evidence.shows: Developers were especially opaque about training data and compute, limiting outside comparisons of their actual methods and the causes of performance differences.

evidence.item: A research preprint studied competition and convergence using Arena and OpenRouter data.
evidence.shows: Developers improved in categories where they lagged competitors while retaining category-specific advantages; the measured frontier also became more crowded. This supports unequal, specialized progress but does not establish that proprietary training methods caused increased methodological divergence.

evidence.item: AP reported that Moonshot's Kimi K3 led an Arena front-end coding ranking while Chinese models competed with leading US systems.
evidence.shows: Labs can lead in particular capabilities, but a single ranking does not establish a longitudinal change in training-method divergence or its cause.

SA-009.thesis: Open models find it increasingly difficult to keep up with the proprietary frontier as key advances become proprietary.
SA-009.bar: Open models fall further behind the proprietary frontier, or take longer to match it, in a way that supports the author's claim that competing has become harder. Proprietary advances are the stated context.
SA-009.actor: Developers of open AI models compared with leading proprietary AI labs.
SA-009.target: A harder time competing than at publication; no numerical gap specified
SA-009.measure: Relative frontier performance and time lag of open models versus leading proprietary models, compared with the June 2024 situation.
SA-009.window: in coming years; no exact end date
indicatorsDecisive: A longitudinal study across a broad, consistent suite of independent evaluations finds a sustained increase in the open-model capability gap or time needed to match proprietary frontier models compared with June 2024.
indicatorsSupporting: Epoch AI benchmarking hub results compare dated open and proprietary releases on multiple tasks.
Model release records measure the delay between proprietary milestones and comparable open models.
Technical reports document whether major frontier training recipes are published or withheld.
indicatorsNo: A broad longitudinal comparison finds open models consistently match the proprietary frontier at least as closely and promptly as in June 2024.
SA-009.measureUsed: Relative performance and time lag of leading open-weight models against leading closed models, compared with June 2024. Epoch AI estimates an average four-month lag and eight-point Epoch Capabilities Index gap in January–May 2026; its 2024 study found benchmark-specific lags of 5–22 months across 13 observations. Stanford's Arena comparison found a seven-point gap in August 2024 and a 49-point gap in March 2026. These estimates use different methods and periods, so the lag figures are not a consistent June-2024-to-2026 comparison.
SA-009.reasoning: The evidence does not establish that open models are further behind, or take longer to catch up, than at the June 2024 baseline. The Arena gap widened after August 2024, but that is a later starting point and one evaluation approach; Epoch's 2026 aggregate lag and its earlier benchmark-specific lags use different methods and cannot settle the change directly. The window remains open, and the mixed evidence leaves the trajectory unclear.

evidence.item: Epoch AI, Open vs. closed AI: How behind are open models?
evidence.shows: Across four benchmarks, 13 measured historical open-model catch-up lags had a 90% interval of 5–22 months; the study also estimated a 15-month training-compute lag. These are historical observations, not a single June 2024 capability-gap estimate.

evidence.item: Epoch AI, Open models lag state-of-the-art closed models by 4 months
evidence.shows: Since January 2026, the leading open-weight models lagged the closed frontier by an average of four months and eight index points on Epoch's aggregate capability measure. The authors identify incomplete benchmark coverage and possible public-benchmark overfitting as limitations.

evidence.item: Stanford AI Index 2026, Technical Performance
evidence.shows: The top open- and closed-weight models were seven Arena points apart in August 2024 and 49 points apart in March 2026, evidence of a later widening on that measure. August follows the June publication baseline, and Arena is only one evaluation approach.

evidence.item: Stanford AI Index 2025, Technical Performance
evidence.shows: The reported Arena gap narrowed from 8.04% in January 2024 to 1.70% in February 2025, evidence against a uniformly widening gap over the broader period.

SA-010.thesis: A model reaches or exceeds in-domain human PhD performance on GPQA in the next one or two model generations.
SA-010.bar: A frontier model reaches at least the benchmark's approximately 80% in-domain expert baseline on a comparable GPQA evaluation within the next one or two model generations.
SA-010.actor: At least one frontier AI model developed by any leading AI lab.
SA-010.measure: GPQA accuracy, compared with the benchmark authors' in-domain PhD expert baseline; use comparable test-set and evaluation conditions.
SA-010.window: in the next generation or two; no calendar date specified
indicatorsDecisive: The GPQA authors or an independent evaluator report at least 80% accuracy for a model from the next one or two generations under conditions comparable to the published expert baseline.
indicatorsSupporting: Epoch AI benchmarking hub tracks GPQA scores by model and evaluation configuration.
Lab system cards report GPQA results, including sampling and prompting methods.
Independent contamination checks and held-out science evaluations assess whether GPQA performance generalizes.
indicatorsNo: Comparable independent GPQA evaluations of the next two model generations remain below the published in-domain expert baseline.
SA-010.measureUsed: Accuracy on the 198-question GPQA Diamond subset. The benchmark authors report 81.3% for expert validators, with selection effects. OpenAI reported 87.7% for the o3 preview on 2024-12-20, or 1.096 times the reading's 80% target. Epoch AI later independently measured 84.8% for a June 2025 Gemini 2.5 Pro preview.
SA-010.reasoning: OpenAI's December 2024 o3 preview exceeded both the fixed 80% target and the benchmark authors' 81.3% Diamond expert figure; o3 was a successor to the post-publication o1 generation. Epoch's later independent result for Gemini 2.5 Pro supports the threshold being reached, although it does not independently reproduce the precise December o3 score. Model and human testing conditions differ, the expert baseline has selection effects, and contamination is a general risk, so this establishes the stated benchmark milestone rather than broad equivalence to PhD experts.

evidence.item: GPQA benchmark paper
evidence.shows: The authors report 81.3% expert-validator accuracy on GPQA Diamond and caution that the subset's validator accuracy is affected by selection.

evidence.item: OpenAI o3 preview announcement reporting
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported 87.7% on GPQA Diamond for o3. The result came from OpenAI's internal evaluation and the model was still a preview.

evidence.item: Independent comparison of GPQA Diamond scores
evidence.shows: Epoch independently measured 84.8% for the June 2025 Gemini 2.5 Pro preview, compared with Google's reported 86.4%; the estimates were consistent within Epoch's uncertainty interval.

evidence.item: Reporting on benchmark contamination
evidence.shows: Public benchmark content can enter model training data, making benchmark results an imperfect measure of generalization.

SA-011.thesis: Giving models more effective inference-time reasoning improves their performance on difficult tasks.
SA-011.bar: A model performs better on difficult tasks when given more effective inference-time reasoning, with evidence isolating the contribution of that additional reasoning.
SA-011.actor: At least one AI model and its developers.
SA-011.window: coming model generations; no exact calendar date
indicatorsDecisive: A controlled evaluation of the same model on a difficult held-out task suite shows higher success with additional inference-time reasoning than with a shorter reasoning budget.
indicatorsSupporting: METR reports dated 50% and 80% task-length success horizons for models using different inference budgets.
Lab technical reports plot difficult-problem accuracy against test-time compute.
Deployment logs or case studies document agents revising solutions and correcting errors on complex tasks.
indicatorsNo: Controlled comparisons across relevant difficult-task evaluations show no improvement from additional effective inference-time reasoning.
SA-011.measureUsed: Performance on difficult tasks by the same model under different inference-time reasoning budgets. OpenAI reported that o1's AIME accuracy increased with test-time compute in September 2024. Independent researchers reported s1-32B AIME 2024 accuracy rising from 50% without budget forcing to 57% with extended reasoning in January 2025.
SA-011.reasoning: Same-model comparisons show that additional inference-time reasoning improved difficult-task performance after publication, and the independent s1 study corroborates the lab evidence. The evidence covers mathematics and competitive programming; it does not establish that every extra reasoning step helps or that gains continue indefinitely. The NeurIPS findings qualify the generality of the effect but do not overturn the documented improvements required by this reading. January 2025 is the first month in the cited evidence by which the result and independent corroboration were available.

evidence.item: OpenAI o1 test-time compute evaluation
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported that o1 performance on difficult mathematics improved as it spent more test-time compute thinking.

evidence.item: s1: Simple test-time scaling
evidence.shows: In an independent controlled intervention on s1-32B, extending its reasoning using budget forcing increased reported AIME 2024 accuracy from 50% to 57%.

evidence.item: OpenAI o3-mini reasoning-effort evaluations
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported progressively higher competitive-programming performance for the same model at greater reasoning effort, providing evidence in a domain beyond mathematics.

evidence.item: gpt-oss model-card reasoning-effort comparison
evidence.shows: For gpt-oss-120b, OpenAI reported AIME 2025 accuracy of 50.4%, 80.0%, and 92.5% at low, medium, and high reasoning effort respectively.

evidence.item: Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
evidence.shows: Across models and benchmarks, the authors found initial improvements followed by declines from overthinking, and argued that some apparent gains depend on the evaluation metric.

SA-012.thesis: Models learn to operate a computer through its interface in a human-like way.
SA-012.bar: A model can operate a computer through its general interface across ordinary applications and tasks, as described by the author. The examples illustrate the breadth of use rather than a mandatory checklist of specific products.
SA-012.actor: At least one multimodal AI system and its developers.
SA-012.window: soon, within the agent transition; no exact calendar date
indicatorsDecisive: An independent evaluation demonstrates a model using a standard graphical computer interface across a broad set of ordinary communication, browsing, document and application workflows.
indicatorsSupporting: OSWorld or a comparable computer-use benchmark reports task completion across applications.
Product documentation and interaction logs show model operation of a desktop interface.
Independent deployment studies document usage across several workplace applications.
indicatorsNo: Computer-use evaluations show models restricted to isolated tools or unable to complete ordinary cross-application interface tasks.
SA-012.measureUsed: Evidence of multimodal agents controlling graphical interfaces across ordinary applications and tasks; no numerical success threshold is specified. Anthropic reported 66.26% on OSWorld for Claude Opus 4.5 in November 2025. OSWorld covers 369 desktop and web tasks, including file operations and multi-application workflows.
SA-012.reasoning: By November 2025, the reported OSWorld result and the independently documented breadth of that benchmark together showed an agent operating a standard graphical interface across a substantial range of desktop and web tasks. Later evaluations show meaningful capability on longer workflows, but also serious reliability weaknesses, especially across multiple applications. Those weaknesses qualify the result; the reading does not require human-level reliability or successful completion of every example.

evidence.item: Claude Opus 4.5 system card
evidence.shows: Anthropic reports 66.26% task completion on OSWorld using the benchmark's default 100-step setting, demonstrating substantial general computer-interface capability.

evidence.item: OSWorld benchmark paper
evidence.shows: The independent benchmark uses real desktop and web applications, file operations and multi-application workflows across 369 tasks, providing context for the later model result.

evidence.item: GPT-5.4 release
evidence.shows: OpenAI describes native computer use for operating computers and workflows across applications, offering further evidence of the capability.

evidence.item: WindowsWorld independent evaluation
evidence.shows: On 181 professional tasks spanning 17 desktop applications, tested agents achieved under 21% success on multi-application tasks and struggled especially with conditional reasoning across three or more applications.

evidence.item: OSWorld 2.0 independent evaluation
evidence.shows: On 108 longer workflows, the authors report that Claude Opus 4.8 completed 20.6% under their primary 500-step setting, although it made partial progress on more tasks. The benchmark includes workflows involving email, documents and applications.

SA-013.thesis: AI agents can submit code changes for human review.
SA-013.bar: An AI agent produces code changes and submits them as a pull request or equivalent reviewable change. This claim does not require the full drop-in-worker capability tracked separately.
SA-013.actor: At least one AI agent used in a software-development workflow.
indicatorsDecisive: A repository audit trail documents an AI agent creating a pull request with its own code changes for review.
indicatorsSupporting: SWE-bench evaluations show agents generating patches for real repository issues.
Agent product documentation describes repository access and pull-request submission.
Deployment logs show agents editing code and running tests before proposing changes.
indicatorsNo: Through 2027, documented agents can suggest code only in chat and cannot submit a reviewable repository change.
SA-013.measureUsed: A documented AI coding agent producing code changes and submitting a pull request or equivalent reviewable change.
SA-013.reasoning: The in-window evidence supports a Hit: GitHub described its agent submitting pull requests, and independent research documented agent-authored pull requests in real repositories. The Tier 1 Codex system card corroborates agent-generated code changes and their availability for pull-request review, though its described submission step involves the user. The March 2024 repository record indicates the capability also existed before publication; it is used for that flag, not to establish the in-window Hit. The resolved date is the earliest in-window date established by the cited evidence, not a claim that no earlier in-window example existed.
SA-013.readingFlag: The reading marks the claim as not already true at publication, but the March 2024 Devin repository audit trail indicates that its stated bar had already been met.

evidence.item: Devin pull request on the mprocs repository
evidence.shows: The devinbot account submitted a pull request with one commit changing three files. The repository owner subsequently discussed the proposed implementation and closed the request; acceptance was not required by the reading.

evidence.item: Codex system card
evidence.shows: OpenAI describes a software-engineering agent trained to generate code and run tests, with generated changes exportable as a GitHub pull request. The card describes a user converting the diff, so it supports the capability without independently establishing agent-created submission.

evidence.item: GitHub Copilot coding-agent announcement
evidence.shows: GitHub describes assigning an issue to its coding agent, which works in the background and submits a pull request for review.

evidence.item: Empirical study of autonomous coding agents in software engineering
evidence.shows: The researchers report a dataset of more than 456,000 pull requests involving five coding agents across real GitHub repositories, corroborating in-window use.

evidence.item: Empirical study of failed agentic pull requests
evidence.shows: The study examined approximately 33,000 agent-authored pull requests and found rejected changes involving failures such as build problems, unwanted changes and logical errors. Those limitations do not negate the ability to submit changes for review.

SA-014.thesis: Agents independently complete large projects requiring weeks of human-equivalent work.
SA-014.bar: An agent can independently complete substantial projects that would take a human weeks, including the necessary planning and correction. A demonstration of isolated short tasks or only generating a long stream of tokens is insufficient.
SA-014.measure: Human-expert completion time for projects independently completed by an AI agent, with success rates and model date reported.
indicatorsDecisive: A representative independent evaluation shows an agent reliably completing projects benchmarked at weeks of human work, with minimal human intervention.
indicatorsSupporting: METR publishes dated 50% and 80% success task horizons for the model.
Independent long-task evaluations document completion and intervention rates on multi-stage projects.
Deployment records show agents planning, testing and correcting work across extended projects.
indicatorsNo: METR and other independent long-task evaluations through 2027 show reliable autonomous completion limited to tasks substantially shorter than weeks.
Audited weeks-scale project attempts consistently require substantive human planning or rescue.
SA-014.measureUsed: Expert-estimated human completion time for autonomously completed software projects, alongside end-to-end success rates. Epoch AI's MirrorCode evaluation estimated 2–17 weeks for one substantial reimplementation; its leaderboard, updated 2026-11-02, reported 97.8% ± 1.5% complete solves across medium and large program tasks for Claude Sonnet 5.5. METR also describes medium-to-large MirrorCode tasks as taking human experts weeks to months. The human-time estimates are uncertain, and the projects have detailed, testable specifications.
SA-014.reasoning: The fixed reading requires at least one agent to complete substantial weeks-scale projects; it does not require reliable completion across all types of project. MirrorCode provides end-to-end autonomous project evidence with high success rates, and METR independently reports additional days-to-weeks-scale evaluation results, although METR and Epoch co-developed MirrorCode and its human-time estimates are imprecise. Broader tasks remain substantially harder, so the result should not be generalized to ordinary projects indiscriminately. November 2 is a documented date by which the bar was met, not necessarily the first day it was met.

evidence.item: MirrorCode preliminary results
evidence.shows: Claude Opus 4.6 autonomously reimplemented a roughly 16,000-line bioinformatics toolkit. Four informal expert estimates of the human time required ranged from 1.5–2.5 weeks to 13–17 weeks; the implementation passed 101 of 102 hidden tests and all visible tests.

evidence.item: MirrorCode benchmark leaderboard
evidence.shows: Claude Sonnet 5.5 scored 97.8% ± 1.5% on complete solves across 15 medium and large programs in two languages, with three runs per task. Agents devised and tested end-to-end implementations without access to the original source code or internet; hidden tests were used for scoring.

evidence.item: AI R&D-relevant model capabilities update
evidence.shows: METR describes medium-to-large MirrorCode programs as taking human experts weeks to months and reports strong autonomous performance. It also finds that recent models beat human baseliners on some days-to-weeks-long machine-learning evaluations with programmatic scoring.

evidence.item: METR combined time-horizon and research-task results
evidence.shows: On the broader TH1.1 plus TH2 suite, METR estimates 50% horizons of 40 hours for GPT-6 Astra and 39 hours for Claude Opus 5.5, with very wide confidence intervals. It also reports that Google DeepMind found 13% success on week-or-longer research tasks, illustrating substantial variation across task types.

SA-015.thesis: A remote AI employee can be onboarded into ordinary company workflows.
SA-015.bar: An agent can be onboarded like a human hire, acquire relevant company context, and participate in ordinary communication and software workflows as a remote coworker. The broader drop-in-worker definition supplies context; the separate pull-request and weeks-long-project claims are not additional requirements here.
SA-015.actor: At least one employer deploying an AI agent as a remote coworker.
indicatorsDecisive: An independently documented workplace deployment shows an agent onboarded with company context and then participating in ordinary team communication and software workflows as a remote coworker.
indicatorsSupporting: Product and deployment documentation show agents ingesting company documents and relevant internal context.
Workplace studies report agents using team messaging and multiple business applications.
METR reports dated model task horizons and success rates for workplace-relevant tasks.
indicatorsNo: Audited deployments through 2027 show agents cannot retain or use company context and require bespoke workflow rebuilding instead of ordinary employee onboarding.
SA-015.measureUsed: A documented deployment in which an agent receives relevant company context and participates with human coworkers in ordinary communications and software workflows.
SA-015.reasoning: By May 2026, Mona had been given the café's lease and operating instructions and was working with human staff through Slack and online business services; AP independently documented the deployment. WIRED's separate reporting on Pronto Housing corroborates the broader pattern of agents participating as coworkers in communication and software workflows. Mona's lost context and mistakes are meaningful limits, but the fixed bar does not require reliable independent completion of weeks-long projects or error-free performance; the experimental setting likewise does not exclude the documented deployment.

evidence.item: Andon Labs described giving its café agent Mona the lease and instructions to operate the business.
evidence.shows: Mona used the lease to identify operational requirements, worked with staff through Slack, and used online services to set up the café. This is the deploying organization's account of the initial context and setup, rather than independent verification.

evidence.item: Associated Press reported on the operating Andon Café in Stockholm and interviewed a human barista.
evidence.shows: Mona communicated with baristas on Slack, advertised jobs on LinkedIn and Indeed, established supplier accounts and managed inventory. It also made serious ordering mistakes and sometimes messaged staff outside working hours; its operator attributed some ordering problems to lost context.

evidence.item: WIRED reported on AI agents used by Pronto Housing, including an engineering agent and a chief-of-staff agent.
evidence.shows: The agents participated in workplace communications and tasks including contracts, scheduling and customer follow-ups. The chief-of-staff agent also mistakenly posted calendar details in Slack, illustrating a practical limitation.

evidence.item: METR reported time-horizon evaluations of models assessed in February and March 2026.
evidence.shows: For the strongest shared model, the estimated 50% horizon was 16–20 hours and the 80% horizon was 3–4 hours on its software-task suite; METR cautioned that the suite could not reliably measure horizons above 16 hours. These results limit conclusions about long autonomous projects, which the fixed reading excludes from this claim.

SA-016.thesis: When drop-in remote workers become easy to integrate, the economic value generated by AI jumps because deployment is easier than for intermediate models.
SA-016.bar: After reliable drop-in agents capable of substantial remote work become available, measured AI-generated economic value rises discontinuously or markedly faster as their easy integration enables deployment. Credible analysis linking the change to that integration is sufficient.
SA-016.actor: Employers adopting drop-in AI remote workers and the suppliers providing them.
SA-016.target: A somewhat discontinuous increase; no numerical amount specified
SA-016.measure: Economic value generated by AI over time, compared around the availability and integration of drop-in remote workers.
SA-016.window: when the drop-in remote worker becomes available; no exact date
indicatorsDecisive: A credible longitudinal economic analysis identifies a discrete jump in AI-generated value around drop-in-worker deployment and links it to easier integration.
indicatorsSupporting: Company filings and surveys measure adoption of drop-in agents and time needed to integrate them.
BEA productivity and value-added data, supplemented by firm-level studies, show changes in affected industries.
BLS employment and wage data and JOLTS vacancies track changes in remote-capable occupations.
AI provider revenue filings and customer reports measure economic uptake.
indicatorsNo: After the trigger, credible longitudinal analyses find AI-generated value grows smoothly without the claimed jump as agents are integrated.
SA-016.condition: Reliable agents capable of replacing substantial remote work become available.
SA-016.measureUsed: Change in AI-generated economic value around the availability and integration of reliable drop-in remote workers. No comparable before-and-after estimate tied to such deployment was identified. As partial indicators, McKinsey's 2026 survey found 37% of respondents attributed some enterprise EBIT impact to AI, approximately unchanged from 2025; the Federal Reserve concluded that generative AI's contribution to aggregate productivity growth thus far was likely small.
SA-016.reasoning: Agents are improving and firms report real benefits, but the evidence does not yet establish that reliable, easily onboarded agents capable of independently completing substantial remote-work projects are generally available. Nor does it establish a marked acceleration or discontinuity in AI-generated economic value linked to their integration; existing surveys and productivity evidence concern a broader mix of AI uses. The condition and undated window remain open, and the speed and economic effects of future deployment are too uncertain for a directional trajectory.

evidence.item: METR capability update
evidence.shows: Frontier agents performed strongly on some autonomous optimization tasks that METR estimated would take dedicated human participants 90–180 hours. METR also reported continuing capability limitations and projected, by naive extrapolation, a 200-hour 50% task-completion horizon in July 2027. These results show progress but do not establish a reliable, generally onboardable remote employee.

evidence.item: METR task-completion time horizons
evidence.shows: The canonical horizon measures predicted success against human expert task duration, chiefly on self-contained software, machine-learning and cybersecurity tasks. METR cautions that ordinary work often requires context absent from its tasks.

evidence.item: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
evidence.shows: The Federal Reserve review finds evidence of task-level efficiency gains, but says their scaling to firms and the economy remains uncertain and that generative AI's contribution to aggregate productivity growth thus far is likely small.

evidence.item: State of AI global survey
evidence.shows: Among respondents at larger organizations, the share scaling agents in at least one function rose from 27% to 40%; 80% of respondents reported individual productivity improvements. However, the share reporting any enterprise EBIT impact from AI remained approximately unchanged at 37%, and the share reporting significant impact of at least 5% of EBIT remained about 6%.

evidence.item: Survey of corporate executives on AI and the workplace
evidence.shows: Executives reported realized AI benefits in efficiency and output, with larger effects expected in 2026 than in 2025. This supports meaningful economic uptake, though it does not establish a discontinuity caused by integrating drop-in workers.

SA-017.thesis: AI broadly outperforms many college graduates in thinking and reasoning by 2025–2026.
SA-017.bar: AI systems outperform a substantial number of college graduates across a broad range of thinking and reasoning tasks. One high score on a single exam or narrow domain is not sufficient.
SA-017.actor: At least one frontier AI system developed by any leading AI lab.
indicatorsDecisive: Independent evaluations across a broad and representative cognitive task suite show a system outperforming a substantial comparison group of college graduates under comparable conditions.
indicatorsSupporting: Benchmark authors' published human baselines and lab system cards compare model and graduate performance across several subjects.
Independent evaluations measure reasoning on unfamiliar, contamination-resistant tasks.
Workplace deployment studies compare model and graduate performance on diverse cognitive assignments.
indicatorsNo: Broad, comparable evaluations through 2026 show frontier systems generally below college graduates across the tested range, despite isolated strengths.
SA-017.measureUsed: Performance across higher-order cognitive assessments and expert-graded professional work products, compared with published human baselines. On GDPval, GPT-5.4 matched or exceeded expert deliverables in 83.0% of comparisons in March 2026; this figure combines wins and ties.
SA-017.reasoning: Taken together, the broad professional-task comparison and independent cognitive assessments support the claim that frontier AI outperforms many college graduates across a range of thinking and reasoning tasks. GPT-5.4's March 2026 result supplies a strong comparison with experienced professionals, while the independent study supplies additional evidence across cognitive domains. The conclusion has limits: GDPval's 83% includes ties, the cognitive study relies partly on historical comparison groups, and the STEM study shows meaningful weaknesses in an older model.

evidence.item: GPT-5.4 GDPval evaluation
evidence.shows: OpenAI reported that GPT-5.4 matched or exceeded industry professionals in 83.0% of comparisons on well-specified knowledge-work tasks spanning 44 occupations. The result combines ties and wins and does not establish that the model outperformed 83% of individual professionals.

evidence.item: Independent comparison of o1-preview with human cognitive-assessment results
evidence.shows: Across several higher-order thinking domains, o1-preview exceeded published human comparison scores on tasks including critical and systematic thinking, data literacy, creativity and logical reasoning. The authors also found limitations in problem-solving and adaptive reasoning; some comparisons used separately collected human baselines and structured assessments.

evidence.item: GDPval benchmark design and initial results
evidence.shows: The benchmark uses blind expert comparisons of human and model work products across 44 occupations; its initial 220-task evaluation found Claude Opus 4.1 matched or exceeded experts on just under half the tasks. The authors caution that inference-time cost and speed figures exclude human oversight and integration.

evidence.item: Human and AI comparison on university STEM assessments
evidence.shows: On 201 university-level STEM questions, the best tested model averaged 58.5% using majority-vote aggregation; students consistently outperformed models on questions involving visual components. The best tested model was GPT-4o, so this does not directly test the later GPT-5.4.

evidence.item: Assessment of human-like intelligence benchmarks
evidence.shows: Researchers identified weaknesses in common benchmarks, including inadequate human validation, poor representation of human variability and simplified tasks. These limitations make broad human–AI comparisons less certain.

SA-018.thesis: Proto-automated AI researchers can automate more than 90% of AI research work.
SA-018.bar: AI systems can perform more than 90% of the relevant AI research work, even if the remaining human bottlenecks prevent full automation. An isolated coding benchmark does not establish the share.
SA-018.actor: AI systems performing research work at a leading AI lab.
SA-018.target: More than 90% of AI research work
SA-018.measure: Share of the work of AI researchers and engineers at a leading lab that AI systems can automate, including the research cycle described in the essay.
indicatorsDecisive: An independently audited, representative task and time study at a leading AI lab establishes that AI systems can perform more than 90% of its researcher and engineer work.
indicatorsSupporting: Lab workflow studies measure AI completion and human intervention across research tasks.
METR reports dated 50% and 80% task horizons for relevant models.
Independent evaluations test novel research idea generation, experimental implementation and result interpretation.
indicatorsNo: Representative audits through 2028 show systems unable to perform more than 90% of leading-lab research work.
SA-018.measureUsed: Share of AI researchers’ and engineers’ work at a leading lab that AI systems can perform, including the research cycle. No available estimate establishes that share on the reading’s definition. Anthropic’s August 2026 index reports AI leading 26% of weighted R&D work and collaborating or better on over 90%; neither figure directly measures the share of work that can be automated as defined in the reading.
SA-018.reasoning: The available leading-lab evidence does not establish that AI can perform more than 90% of the relevant research and engineering work. Anthropic’s over-90% collaboration figure includes close human direction, while its 26% leadership figure and OpenAI’s task success rates use different measures from the target. The window has not begun, and rapid capability gains make the eventual outcome uncertain; the evidence does not support a reliable ratio to the target.

evidence.item: Anthropic R&D Automation Index
evidence.shows: Anthropic reports that Claude leads 26% of its weighted AI R&D work, meaning it completes most of a task from a high-level prompt with human supervision. Claude collaborates or better on over 90%, but collaboration includes large chunks of work under close human direction. The index uses model-assigned ratings and approximate person-time weights.

evidence.item: OpenAI research workflow analysis
evidence.shows: Estimated autonomous success on research tasks requiring two to four human hours rose from 23% in March to 46% in October; success on four-to-eight-hour tasks rose from 13% to 35%. These are task success rates, not a measured share of all research work.

evidence.item: METR AI R&D capability update
evidence.shows: METR reports that time horizons on its combined task suites doubled roughly every 3.6 months, while cautioning that task composition and measurement uncertainty affect interpretation. This is evidence of rapid progress, not a direct measure of the share of lab research work automated.

evidence.item: FIRE-Bench full-cycle research evaluation
evidence.shows: In an evaluation requiring agents to design experiments, execute them and draw evidence-backed conclusions from published machine-learning research questions, the strongest tested agent achieved under 50 F1 on rediscovery, with recurring experimental and reasoning failures.

evidence.item: Anthropic staff survey
evidence.shows: In an August survey, the median staff estimate was that AI did 51% of the work of building an early-2026 frontier model at the time, with a forecast of 80% by the end of 2027. These are personal estimates and forecasts, not an audit or a direct measure of the stated target.

SA-019.thesis: Partial automation of AI research accelerates the pace of AI progress by at least 3×.
SA-019.bar: Partial automated research increases the rate of AI research progress to at least three times its comparable pre-automation rate. Credible analysis linking that acceleration to automation is sufficient.
SA-019.actor: Leading AI labs using proto-automated researchers.
SA-019.measure: Rate of algorithmic AI progress at a leading lab relative to its pre-automation rate, using comparable effective-compute efficiency gains per unit time.
indicatorsDecisive: A credible longitudinal lab analysis measures at least a 3× increase in comparable algorithmic efficiency gains per year and links the acceleration to partially automated research.
indicatorsSupporting: Lab research records quantify the share of experiments and research tasks performed by AI.
Controlled scaling studies estimate training-efficiency improvements over time.
Independent reports document AI-authored contributions adopted in frontier training recipes.
indicatorsNo: Comparable progress-rate estimates through 2028 remain below 3× the pre-automation rate, even where partial research automation is deployed.
SA-019.measureUsed: Acceleration in comparable algorithmic training-efficiency gains per unit time at a leading lab, relative to its pre-automation rate. No public estimate establishes this ratio as of 2026-11-23. METR estimates a 1.9× acceleration in Anthropic's benchmark-based capability index since October 2025, but that is a different measure and cannot be divided by the 3× target as though it were a training-compute-efficiency estimate.
SA-019.reasoning: Partial research automation is documented, and METR finds substantial AI-linked acceleration at Anthropic, but the public evidence does not establish a 3× increase on the reading's comparable training-efficiency measure. The strongest numerical estimates concern capability benchmarks or researchers' self-reported output, which are informative but not interchangeable with effective-compute gains per year. The window remains open through 2028; the evidence supports a possible future hit, but uncertainty about the relevant efficiency rate and its trajectory makes the trajectory unclear.

evidence.item: Independent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic
evidence.shows: METR reviewed internal training, compute, algorithmic-efficiency and benchmark data. It estimated that Anthropic's capability index was advancing 1.9× as fast as before October 2025, with a 95% interval of 1.5–2.8×, and judged that AI use likely accounted for most of the current acceleration. Some redacted internal evidence suggested acceleration above 2× and increasing, but METR emphasized substantial uncertainty. The published 1.9× figure is a capability-index trend, not the specified algorithmic-efficiency rate.

evidence.item: Research acceleration: The jagged frontier
evidence.shows: OpenAI reports that surveyed researchers estimated their teams would need a median of three months to match one month of recent work without advanced coding agents. This is a self-reported work-output counterfactual, not a measured 3× increase in algorithmic efficiency. OpenAI also reports its capability index rose 16.4 points per year since August 2025; that figure does not establish a comparable pre-automation efficiency-rate ratio.

evidence.item: Have AI capabilities accelerated?
evidence.shows: Epoch finds acceleration on three of four capability metrics, associated with reasoning models. Capability trends alone do not isolate improvements in training-compute efficiency or attribute them to research automation.

evidence.item: METR sensitivity analysis of Anthropic's capability trend
evidence.shows: Reasonable alternative statistical link functions produce estimated capability accelerations from 1.1× to 2.9×, with similar fit. METR also identifies possible non-AI causes and benchmark-specific distortions, limiting confidence in translating the capability estimate into the stated causal efficiency measure.

SA-020.thesis: The transition from nearly automated AI research work to full automation takes only a few years.
SA-020.bar: Once systems can replace most researcher or engineer work but still need some supervision, full automation of that work follows within the author's few-years interval. The essay does not give an exact numerical cutoff.
SA-020.actor: Any leading AI lab developing automated AI researchers or engineers.
SA-020.target: A few years from near-automation to full automation; no exact numerical bound specified
SA-020.measure: Elapsed time between an AI system performing almost all researcher or engineer work with some human supervision and one fully performing that work.
SA-020.window: after the almost-replacement phase; no fixed calendar dates
indicatorsDecisive: Dated, independently audited lab deployments establish near-replacement and then full performance of the researcher or engineer job within a few years.
indicatorsSupporting: Representative workflow audits estimate the remaining share of research tasks requiring humans.
METR publishes dated task horizons for successive systems.
Lab reports document whether formerly human-only research decisions and supervision are automated.
indicatorsNo: A documented near-replacement system is followed by more than a few years without a system able to perform the full job.
SA-020.condition: Systems can already replace most researcher or engineer work while still requiring some human supervision.
SA-020.measureUsed: Elapsed time from a system performing almost all of an AI researcher’s or engineer’s job with some supervision to a system fully performing that job. Neither endpoint has been established well enough to calculate an elapsed time.
SA-020.reasoning: Available evidence shows rapid progress on research tasks and some end-to-end demonstrations, but does not establish either near-replacement of most of a researcher or engineer’s job or subsequent full automation. The condition remains possible and the window has no fixed end, so the claim is not yet resolved. Task-horizon trends support continued progress, but uneven research capabilities and the absence of a dated starting point make the trajectory for the specified transition unclear.

evidence.item: Anthropic R&D Automation Index
evidence.shows: Anthropic reported that Claude led 26% of its measured model R&D tasks in August 2026, up from under 1% in February. This is evidence of substantial supervised automation, but 26% does not establish replacement of most of the job.

evidence.item: Research acceleration: The jagged frontier
evidence.shows: OpenAI estimated that agents completed 46% of research tasks requiring two to four human hours without intervention in October, up from 23% in March. The result concerns selected tasks, not full researcher jobs; OpenAI says humans remain central to development.

evidence.item: AI R&D-relevant model capabilities are improving rapidly and are getting harder to measure
evidence.shows: METR reports a roughly 3.6-month doubling time for task horizons on its combined suites, but says public models still have deficiencies that prevent full automation of tasks involved in AI research. Its tasks and estimated horizons do not measure an entire job.

evidence.item: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies
evidence.shows: In two research case studies, agents completed the engineering without human help but did not make substantial progress on the central research questions. The small sample limits generalization, but illustrates a remaining research-cycle gap.

evidence.item: Towards end-to-end automation of AI research
evidence.shows: The AI Scientist generated and tested research ideas and produced a paper that exceeded the average acceptance threshold at a workshop. This demonstrates an end-to-end research workflow in a constrained setting, not full performance of a frontier researcher’s job.

SA-021.thesis: A large workforce of automated AI researchers compresses a decade of algorithmic progress into at most one year.
SA-021.bar: Once a large effective automated research workforce is supported by compute, it produces at least 5 OOMs of algorithmic efficiency gains within one year. Credible evidence should connect the gains to the automated research workforce.
SA-021.actor: Any leading AI lab operating a large workforce of effective automated AI researchers.
SA-021.target: At least 5 orders of magnitude, or 100,000×, in algorithmic effective-compute gains within at most 1 year
SA-021.measure: Within-paradigm training-compute efficiency gain from automated AI research over a one-year interval, compared with the prior roughly 0.5 OOM per year trend.
SA-021.window: after full AI research automation, in a year or less; no fixed calendar dates
indicatorsDecisive: Controlled training scaling studies and lab research records show at least 100,000× algorithmic training-efficiency gains within a year, credibly attributable to automated AI research.
indicatorsSupporting: Lab records document the number, effectiveness and research output of automated researcher instances.
Training studies measure successive algorithmic efficiency gains against fixed performance targets.
Epoch AI model data and technical reports track training FLOP and the performance of successive models.
indicatorsNo: After the trigger, comparable efficiency studies show less than 5 OOMs of algorithmic gain in the relevant one-year interval.
SA-021.condition: Compute supports large populations of effective automated researchers.
SA-021.measureUsed: Within-paradigm reduction in training compute needed to reach a fixed performance target, attributable to automated AI research, over at most one year. No comparable estimate of the required workforce-attributable gain is available. Epoch AI's historical pretraining estimate was a doubling of efficiency every 5–14 months; it is background context, not an observed post-trigger result.
SA-021.reasoning: The evidence shows meaningful AI contributions to research, but does not establish the specified full-automation trigger or a 100,000× training-compute efficiency gain attributable to an automated research workforce. The condition could still be met and the reading sets no fixed calendar deadline, so the window remains open. Current task-level gains and historical efficiency trends do not provide a defensible estimate of the eventual one-year result or a reliable trajectory toward the threshold.

evidence.item: OpenAI's internal research-acceleration report
evidence.shows: Estimated autonomous success on research tasks requiring two to four hours of human work rose from 23% in March to 46% in October 2026. OpenAI says humans remain central to the research loop; the report does not establish full research automation or a 100,000× training-efficiency gain.

evidence.item: METR evaluation of AI R&D-relevant capabilities
evidence.shows: The best tested agent achieved a 15.7% speedup on a fixed-target NanoGPT training task in 48 hours, while agents outperformed many human speedrunners. This is a limited task and includes systems-level speedups, so it is not a direct estimate of the claim's one-year algorithmic training-compute gain.

evidence.item: Epoch AI InnovationEval
evidence.shows: In an early end-to-end test, frontier agents made little progress toward independently matching a human-developed machine-learning innovation despite substantial GPU expenditure. The result covers one research task and cannot settle all AI research capabilities.

evidence.item: Reporting on Anthropic's research automation
evidence.shows: Anthropic reported that Claude led 26% of its measured model R&D, completing most of a task from a high-level prompt under human supervision. This is evidence of substantial research assistance, not full automation of the research cycle.

evidence.item: Historical study of algorithmic progress in language models
evidence.shows: Epoch estimated that pretraining algorithmic efficiency doubled every 5–14 months. This is a historical baseline, not evidence of the required future AI-attributable gain.

SA-022.thesis: After AI research is fully automated, vastly superhuman systems arrive within a few years.
SA-022.bar: A system vastly smarter than humans, with novel and creative capabilities beyond human understanding across many domains, appears within the author's few-years interval after fully automated frontier AI research. Exceptional performance in one domain alone does not suffice.
SA-022.actor: Any leading AI lab operating fully automated frontier AI research.
SA-022.target: A year to at most a few years, with the author also allowing a few months; no exact numerical upper bound specified
SA-022.measure: Elapsed time from fully automated frontier AI research to vastly superhuman AI.
SA-022.window: after fully automated AI research; no fixed calendar dates
indicatorsDecisive: A broad independent assessment of real-world cognitive work and novel research across many domains establishes vastly superhuman qualitative capability, with dated records placing it within a few years of fully automated frontier AI research.
indicatorsSupporting: Independent evaluations compare model performance with expert human baselines across multiple fields.
Audited research records document novel AI-generated results that expert teams verify.
Deployment and METR long-task evaluations track autonomous performance across increasingly complex projects.
indicatorsNo: More than a few years after documented full automation of frontier AI research, broad evidence still shows no system with the author's vastly superhuman cross-domain capability.
SA-022.condition: Fully automated frontier AI research is achieved.
SA-022.measureUsed: Elapsed time from fully automated frontier AI research to the appearance of a qualitatively vastly superhuman system across many domains. Neither endpoint has been established, so no elapsed time can be calculated.
SA-022.reasoning: The available evidence shows substantial automated research progress, but it does not establish either fully automated frontier AI research at a leading lab or the specified vastly superhuman capability across many domains. The condition could still occur, and the few-years interval has no fixed calendar start or end; the forecast is therefore Not yet, rather than a Miss or Condition not met. The trajectory is unclear because current progress does not establish how quickly the second milestone would follow the first.

evidence.item: METR's independent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic
evidence.shows: A high-access assessment found AI was contributing to research acceleration, primarily through assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions. It does not establish full automation of frontier AI research.

evidence.item: OpenAI's internal research-acceleration measurements
evidence.shows: Estimated autonomous success on research tasks requiring two to four hours of human work rose from 23% in March to 46% in October 2026; OpenAI reports that humans remain central to its research loop.

evidence.item: METR update on AI R&D-relevant capabilities
evidence.shows: METR reports rapidly improving public-model capabilities but also limitations on tasks requiring judgment or lacking clear feedback, which may impede extensive research automation.

evidence.item: Peer-reviewed study of The AI Scientist
evidence.shows: An automated pipeline generated machine-learning research papers, one of which exceeded the average human acceptance threshold at a workshop. This is evidence of autonomous research progress, but does not establish fully automated frontier lab research or vastly superhuman capability across domains.

evidence.item: Scientist World research benchmark preprint
evidence.shows: The authors report that frontier AI scientists surpassed reproduced human-research baselines 74% of the time in their research environments. This is a promising but narrower benchmark result than the claimed cross-domain qualitative capability.

SA-023.thesis: Superintelligence arrives by the end of 2029.
SA-023.bar: By the end of 2029, an AI system is vastly smarter than humans and capable of novel, creative and complicated behavior beyond human understanding across many domains. Human-level AI or a narrow superhuman system alone is insufficient.
SA-023.actor: At least one AI system developed by any leading AI lab.
SA-023.window: by the end of the decade
indicatorsDecisive: An independent assessment spanning many cognitive domains and novel real-world problems establishes the author's qualitatively and vastly superhuman level by the end of 2029.
indicatorsSupporting: Expert-baselined evaluations show performance far above leading humans across diverse fields.
Independent expert teams verify novel AI-generated scientific and technical results.
Deployment and METR long-task evaluations document autonomous work on complex projects across domains.
indicatorsNo: Comprehensive evidence through 2029 shows no AI system with the author's vastly superhuman, cross-domain capabilities.
SA-023.measureUsed: Qualitative evidence of AI vastly exceeding humans in novel, creative, complicated behavior across many domains, assessed through expert comparisons, scientific results, and autonomous-task evaluations as of 2026-11-23.
SA-023.reasoning: Evidence shows remarkable advances, including novel mathematical research and strong autonomous performance, but it does not yet establish behavior vastly beyond human understanding across many domains. METR's expert comparisons and the cross-domain scientific evaluation also document material limitations; they do not rule out stronger undisclosed systems. The window remains open through 2029, and rapid progress makes the trajectory uncertain rather than clearly on or off track.

evidence.item: METR evaluated public frontier models on AI research and development tasks, including programming contests and research engineering.
evidence.shows: The strongest models placed at the 96th–98th percentile of participants in the median optimization contest, but roughly four humans beat them in the median contest. METR also found weaknesses in judgment where clear empirical feedback was unavailable. These are substantial capabilities but do not establish the specified vast cross-domain superiority.

evidence.item: EurekaBench evaluated AI agents on 26 expert-verified scientific tasks across six fields.
evidence.shows: The authors report that agents sometimes surpassed human scientists in predictive accuracy but fell substantially short in deriving scientific insights. The study tests an important slice of cross-domain research, not every possible capability.

evidence.item: Quanta reported expert analysis of an AI-generated quasi-Riemann hypothesis result.
evidence.shows: Mathematicians largely agreed that one result was correct and identified a novel combination of existing number-theory ideas. This is strong evidence of novel research capability in mathematics, though it does not establish the required level across many domains.

evidence.item: AP reported a mathematician's claim that he and Claude had proved the Riemann hypothesis.
evidence.shows: The claimed AI-assisted result is evidence of rapid progress on an exceptionally difficult mathematical problem. At the time of AP's report, the claim had only just been announced and the problem remained listed as unsolved by the Clay Mathematics Institute.

evidence.item: METR reported a roughly 3.6-month doubling time in its measured task-completion horizons across two task sets.
evidence.shows: Autonomous capabilities have improved rapidly, but METR cautions that its tasks concern AI research and development and that measuring current models is becoming harder. This trend alone cannot establish when the broader qualitative bar will be met.

SA-024.thesis: Billions of vastly superhuman AI agents can operate by the end of the decade.
SA-024.bar: Infrastructure can operate billions of agent instances whose capabilities meet the author's vastly superhuman, cross-domain definition. Large numbers of weaker agents or a single narrow superhuman system do not meet the bar.
SA-024.actor: Operators of AI inference infrastructure capable of running superintelligent agents.
SA-024.target: Billions of operating vastly superhuman AI agents
SA-024.measure: Number of concurrently operable distinct AI agent instances at the author's superintelligence capability level.
SA-024.window: by the time the decade is out
indicatorsDecisive: Audited deployment or capacity records establish billions of concurrent agent instances, and independent cross-domain assessments establish that those instances have the author's vastly superhuman capabilities.
indicatorsSupporting: Operator and utility filings and Epoch AI data-centre tracking establish inference capacity and power available for agent operation.
Technical reports measure per-agent inference requirements and concurrent serving throughput.
Independent expert evaluations and verified research outputs assess cross-domain superhuman capability.
indicatorsNo: By the end of 2029, independently assessed systems do not meet the author's superintelligence definition.
Credible capacity estimates show that fewer than billions of qualifying agents can operate concurrently.
SA-024.measureUsed: Concurrent distinct agent instances meeting the essay’s vastly superhuman, cross-domain definition. No defensible current count or ratio to billions is available: the capabilities and per-agent serving requirements of a qualifying system have not been established. As capacity context, Epoch AI estimates that agentic inference capacity of AI chips sold to date grew 4.6× from Q2 2025 to Q2 2026; this is a fixed-workload hardware index, not a count of qualifying agents.
SA-024.reasoning: Neither a vastly superhuman cross-domain agent nor capacity to operate billions of such agents concurrently has been established. The evidence shows both substantial capability gains and remaining limitations, while the available capacity measures cannot be converted into a qualifying agent count. The window remains open through 2029; rapid progress makes the trajectory uncertain rather than clearly on or off track.

evidence.item: METR’s Q4 2026 capability update
evidence.shows: Progress is rapid: METR reports a 98% FrontierMath Tier 4 score for GPT-6 Astra and strong autonomous performance on a coding optimization task. But top human contributors achieved larger speedups than the tested agents on that optimization task; these results do not establish vastly superhuman performance across domains.

evidence.item: 2026 AI Index technical performance report
evidence.shows: The report documents rapid gains on difficult benchmarks, while finding uneven performance: its reported top model scored 50.6% on analog clock reading versus 90.1% for humans, and agents remained below the human baseline on OSWorld. These tests predate the latest models and are not a complete assessment of them.

evidence.item: Agentic inference capacity growth estimate
evidence.shows: Epoch estimates a 4.6× increase in agentic inference capacity of AI chips sold to date between Q2 2025 and Q2 2026, using chip sales and a fixed set of inference workloads. It does not estimate concurrent instances of a vastly superhuman agent.

evidence.item: Largest AI data centers by power capacity
evidence.shows: Epoch estimates that the largest tracked operational AI data center had about 1,037 MW of IT power in November 2026. Power capacity alone cannot establish how many qualifying agents can run concurrently.

SA-025.thesis: After AGI is applied to robotics research, solving robotics and scaling production delays broad automation by no more than a few years.
SA-025.bar: Within no more than a few years of the trigger, robotics has ceased to be a barrier to broad automation of physical work, including the physical testing and initial production ramp the author identifies. A single impressive robot or isolated deployment is insufficient.
SA-025.actor: AI and robotics researchers and deployers worldwide, using AGI or superintelligence.
SA-025.target: No more than a few years of delay.
SA-025.measure: Elapsed time from the specified AGI deployment to robotics becoming sufficiently capable and available for broad physical-labor automation.
SA-025.window: After AGI; no more than a few years.
indicatorsDecisive: Industry deployment and production records show robots capable of broadly automating physical work are available at scale within a few years of documented AGI deployment to robotics R&D.
indicatorsSupporting: Independent evaluations show general-purpose robots reliably completing varied real-world work tasks.
Manufacturers’ production and installation records show rapid growth in robot supply.
Published robotics research documents major AI-driven advances in manipulation and mobility.
indicatorsNo: Several years after the trigger, independent deployment and production evidence shows robotics remains a substantial barrier to broad physical-labor automation.
SA-025.condition: AGI is achieved and deployed to robotics R&D.
SA-025.measureUsed: Elapsed time from deployment to robotics R&D of an AI capable of fully doing an AI researcher’s or engineer’s job, until robots are sufficiently capable and available for broad physical-labor automation. Neither endpoint has been established, so elapsed time and a ratio to the unspecified 'few years' cannot be calculated.
SA-025.reasoning: The specified trigger is not established: evidence shows substantial AI assistance in research, but not an AI that can fully do an AI researcher’s or engineer’s job and has been deployed to robotics R&D. Robot deployments and industrial supply have grown, while assessed capabilities still have significant gaps; neither establishes that robotics has ceased to be a barrier to broad physical-labor automation. Because the trigger can still occur, the window remains open, and present trends do not establish how long automation will take after it occurs.

evidence.item: METR, AI R&D-relevant model capabilities are improving rapidly and are getting harder to measure
evidence.shows: METR reports substantial progress but says public frontier models still have deficiencies that prevent them from fully automating tasks involved in AI research work.

evidence.item: Research acceleration: The jagged frontier
evidence.shows: OpenAI reports that autonomous success varies across its research tasks: for August 1 through October 18, estimated success without human intervention was 43% for Build tasks, versus 69% for Communicate and 58% for Analyze tasks.

evidence.item: BMW Group humanoid robot production pilot
evidence.shows: BMW reports that Figure 02 handled repetitive sheet-metal positioning during a ten-month pilot supporting production of more than 30,000 vehicles. This is a real production application but does not establish broad physical-labor automation.

evidence.item: World Robotics 2026 industrial robots executive summary
evidence.shows: The federation reports 603,307 industrial robot installations worldwide in 2025, up 11%, and an operational stock of about 5.08 million. These figures demonstrate production and deployment scale, but do not establish general capability across physical work.

evidence.item: Where autonomy works: evaluating robot capabilities in 2026
evidence.shows: Epoch finds progress on manipulation but describes narrow transfer for precision tasks; it reports that no robot had attempted its full PC-assembly task, although components such as cable insertion had been demonstrated.

SA-026.thesis: Applying superintelligence broadly to research produces extraordinary scientific and technological progress, compressing roughly a century of human R&D into years.
SA-026.bar: Across many scientific and technological fields, superintelligence-driven R&D produces advances in years comparable to what human researchers would otherwise have achieved over approximately a century. The author’s century comparison is a counterfactual judgment, so independent historical and domain-expert evidence must support it.
SA-026.actor: Superintelligent AI researchers, engineers and robot technicians applied across scientific and technological fields worldwide.
SA-026.target: A century of human R&D effort compressed into years.
SA-026.measure: Rate and breadth of substantive scientific and technological advances compared with the historic human research trajectory.
indicatorsDecisive: A cross-field independent assessment of validated discoveries and implemented technologies finds that advances over a few years are comparable in breadth and magnitude to a century of the prior human R&D trajectory, with credible evidence linking the acceleration to superintelligent R&D.
indicatorsSupporting: Independent scientific reviews document major validated discoveries in several unrelated fields.
R&D records show substantial deployment of qualifying superintelligent agents across disciplines.
Patent, publication and technology-deployment records show a sharp acceleration in substantive advances.
indicatorsNo: Cross-field assessments show that scientific and technological progress during the window remains comparable to its historic pace despite broad application of qualifying superintelligence.
SA-026.condition: Superintelligence is broadly applied to scientific R&D.
SA-026.measureUsed: Breadth and magnitude of validated scientific and technological advances over a few years, compared with a counterfactual century of prior human R&D, with credible evidence attributing the acceleration to broadly applied superintelligent R&D. No defensible numerical ratio to that target is currently available.
SA-026.reasoning: As of 2026-11-23, AI is contributing to research, but the evidence does not establish broad deployment of qualifying superintelligence or century-equivalent progress across many fields. The condition could still be met and the 2030s window has not begun, so the outcome is Not yet. The trajectory is unclear: current advances support the possibility of acceleration, but they do not establish its future scale or timing.

evidence.item: International AI Safety Report 2026
evidence.shows: AI systems assist scientific research and perform strongly on some expert benchmarks, but remain uneven, make errors on multistep tasks, and cannot yet automate the complex tasks and long-term planning required for many jobs. The report describes future progress and its effect on research as uncertain.

evidence.item: Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists’ impact but contract science’s focus
evidence.shows: A study of 41.3 million natural-science papers found productivity and impact advantages associated with AI use, alongside a narrowing of collective research focus. It does not establish century-equivalent advances in years.

evidence.item: AI in Science: Early Insights
evidence.shows: A preprint using AI interaction data, an inventory of specialized models, and a survey of scientists reports broad scientific use and substantial self-reported time savings, while noting downstream bottlenecks and limited evidence on ultimate impact.

evidence.item: Practical Use of Advanced AI Frameworks on Real-Life Scientific Problems: Three Case Studies
evidence.shows: Across three real-world research problems, the authors report recurring failures, including omission or substitution of relevant data, limiting the reliability of autonomous research.

SA-027.thesis: Broad cognitive and physical labor automation can enable a shift in the global growth regime to annual economic growth exceeding 30%.
SA-027.bar: At least one annual observation of real global economic growth exceeds 30%, with credible analysis linking the growth to broad labor automation. The essay’s growth-mode table supplies the global-economy context.
SA-027.actor: The world economy, with firms and other organizations deploying automated cognitive and physical labor.
SA-027.measure: Annual real world GDP growth, using a consistent IMF or World Bank world aggregate.
SA-027.window: After broad labor automation; no calendar date specified.
indicatorsDecisive: IMF or World Bank real world GDP data show annual growth above 30%, with credible analysis connecting it to widespread labor automation.
indicatorsSupporting: National accounts show unusually rapid real GDP growth across several major economies.
Employment and production surveys show widespread substitution of automated systems for cognitive and physical labor.
Business investment and robot-installation data show rapid expansion of automated productive capacity.
indicatorsNo: After the trigger, credible global real GDP accounts show growth remains at or below 30% throughout the period under review.
SA-027.condition: Cognitive and physical labor are widely automated and societal frictions permit deployment.
SA-027.measureUsed: World Bank annual real world GDP growth, aggregated using real US-dollar GDP weights at average 2010–2019 prices and market exchange rates: 2.9% in 2024 and an estimated 2.9% in 2025; 2.5% forecast for 2026. The ratio uses the latest completed year's estimate: 2.9/30 = 0.0967.
SA-027.reasoning: The latest completed annual World Bank estimate is 2.9%, far below the required rate above 30%, and there is no credible evidence connecting such a growth rate to broad labor automation. AI and robot adoption have advanced, but the specified broad cognitive and physical labor automation condition remains pending. The window has no calendar deadline, so the trajectory is unclear rather than off track despite current growth being far below the threshold.

evidence.item: World Bank Global Economic Prospects, June 2026
evidence.shows: World real GDP grew 2.9% in 2024 and an estimated 2.9% in 2025; the Bank forecast 2.5% for 2026. These figures are well below 30%.

evidence.item: World Economic Outlook, October 2026
evidence.shows: The IMF separately projected world growth of 3.1% in 2026. This is a forecast using the IMF aggregate, not a completed annual observation on the World Bank measure.

evidence.item: OECD Digital Economy and Society Outlook 2026
evidence.shows: In 2025, 20% of OECD enterprises with at least 10 employees reported AI use, versus 52% of large enterprises. Adoption is increasing but does not establish broad automation of cognitive and physical labor.

evidence.item: World Robotics 2026 industrial robot figures
evidence.shows: Factories installed over 600,000 industrial robots in 2025, and the operational stock reached about 5 million, evidence of expanding physical automation in factories.

evidence.item: Survey of AI use in businesses across four countries
evidence.shows: Roughly 70% of surveyed firms reported some AI adoption, while reported effects on employment and productivity remained small. This broader adoption estimate does not establish widespread labor substitution.

SA-028.thesis: A largest-scale training cluster reaches roughly one million H100-equivalent accelerators around 2026.
SA-028.bar: One operational training cluster has capacity of at least roughly one million H100 equivalents. The 2026 calendar year is the reference year, not a precisely bounded interpretation of “around.”
SA-028.actor: An operator of an individual frontier AI training cluster.
SA-028.measure: AI training compute capacity of one cluster expressed in H100-equivalent accelerators, rather than a fleet-wide physical-chip count.
indicatorsDecisive: Epoch AI data-centre tracking or an operator technical report establishes an operational individual training cluster of at least 1 million H100 equivalents.
indicatorsSupporting: Operator procurement disclosures document accelerator orders sufficient for the cluster.
SemiAnalysis reports document cluster networking, chip deployment and H100-equivalent capacity.
Utility filings show a site has secured power consistent with large-scale training.
indicatorsNo: Epoch AI and operator records establish that the largest operational individual training clusters around the reference year remain below 1 million H100 equivalents.
SA-028.measureUsed: Peak theoretical AI compute capacity of one operational training cluster, expressed in H100 equivalents. Epoch AI lists Colossus 2 at 1.112 million H100 equivalents and Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle at 818,000 H100 equivalents as data-center totals, but those figures do not establish the capacity of one training cluster. An independently processed Epoch GPU-cluster dataset reported a known operational single-cluster record of 275,796 H100 equivalents as of 2026-08-27; that record is not necessarily the largest cluster operating today.
SA-028.reasoning: The largest tracked data center exceeds the numerical target, but its total cannot automatically be assigned to one training cluster; SpaceX's prospectus explicitly describes separate clusters at Colossus II. Amazon confirms a very large operational training cluster at Rainier, but the available evidence does not establish that its individual-cluster capacity has reached the H100-equivalent target. The window remains open, and the scale of deployments and planned expansions makes the year-end trajectory unclear.

evidence.item: Epoch AI data-center tracking
evidence.shows: Lists Colossus 2 at 1.112 million H100 equivalents and Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle at 818,000 H100 equivalents. These are data-center estimates, so neither alone establishes the capacity of an individual training cluster.

evidence.item: Processed Epoch GPU-cluster record
evidence.shows: Reports 275,796 H100 equivalents for the largest qualifying known operational contiguous cluster, xAI Colossus Memphis Phase 3, using Epoch's processed dataset. The record is limited to publicly tracked clusters and the stated retrieval date.

evidence.item: SpaceX prospectus
evidence.shows: States that Colossus II brought online a first cluster of approximately 110,000 GB200 processors and a second cluster of 110,000 GB300 processors, distinguishing individual clusters within the facility.

evidence.item: Amazon earnings release
evidence.shows: Reports that Project Rainier was an operational training cluster with more than 500,000 Trainium2 chips. Physical chip count is not the same as H100-equivalent compute.

SA-029.thesis: An individual frontier training cluster requires about one gigawatt around 2026.
SA-029.bar: An individual operational training cluster requires at least about 1 GW, including supporting datacenter loads. A campus power reservation alone does not establish actual cluster demand.
SA-029.actor: An operator of an individual frontier AI training cluster.
SA-029.measure: Power demand of one AI training cluster, including supporting datacenter loads.
indicatorsDecisive: Operator or utility records establish at least approximately 1 GW of power demand for one operational training cluster.
indicatorsSupporting: Epoch AI or SemiAnalysis identifies a comparably sized training installation.
