SA-040.measureUsed: Annual worldwide capital investment in AI compute infrastructure, including accelerators, data centers and associated power infrastructure. No complete, consistently defined current worldwide estimate was found. Proxies include PwC/Oxford Economics’ forecast of $800 billion in global data-center capex in 2026 and $1.1 trillion in 2030, and IDC’s narrower AI infrastructure forecast of $521 billion in 2026 and $1.33 trillion in 2030. These proxies do not cover precisely the same scope as the claim, particularly associated power infrastructure; the 2030 figures are forecasts, not outcomes.
SA-040.reasoning: The 2030 reference year remains open, and the available evidence does not establish an early achievement of $8 trillion in annual worldwide investment. The trajectory is off track: the identified 2030 forecasts are far below the target, despite rapid spending growth and Gartner’s higher near-term infrastructure estimate. Their differing scopes and uncertain treatment of associated power mean none is an exact outcome-to-target comparison, and projections can change before 2030.

evidence.item: Amazon third-quarter results
evidence.shows: Amazon maintained guidance of approximately $220 billion in company-wide cash capital expenditures for 2026. This is a partial indicator and includes spending outside AI infrastructure.

evidence.item: Alphabet third-quarter earnings call
evidence.shows: Alphabet reported $51.4 billion of third-quarter capex, the vast majority for technical infrastructure supporting AI, and maintained 2026 company-wide capex guidance of $195 billion to $205 billion.

evidence.item: Worldwide AI spending forecast
evidence.shows: Gartner forecasts $1.563 trillion in AI infrastructure spending in 2026 and $2.397 trillion in 2027. This broader spending category is not established as a non-double-counted estimate of the reading’s capital-investment measure.

evidence.item: Global Data Centre Outlook
evidence.shows: PwC and Oxford Economics project global data-center capex, including computing equipment, at roughly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.1 trillion in 2030. The 2030 forecast is 0.1375 of the target, but includes non-AI data centers and does not establish coverage of all associated power investment.

evidence.item: Worldwide Quarterly AI Infrastructure Tracker
evidence.shows: IDC reports $121.4 billion in AI infrastructure spending in the second quarter of 2026 and forecasts $521 billion for 2026 and $1.33 trillion for 2030. Its narrower infrastructure market forecast is not a complete estimate of the claim’s data-center and power scope.

evidence.item: Global data-center investment outlook
evidence.shows: McKinsey estimates global data-center spending could reach $7 trillion cumulatively from 2025 through 2030, much of it AI-driven; that is a multi-year total, not an annual 2030 figure.

SA-041.thesis: Worldwide annual AI accelerator production reaches hundreds of millions of H100 equivalents around 2030.
SA-041.bar: Worldwide annual shipments of AI accelerators reach hundreds of millions of H100 equivalents. The table’s measure is performance-equivalent shipments rather than necessarily hundreds of millions of physical chips.
SA-041.actor: AI accelerator manufacturers and their fabrication and packaging suppliers worldwide.
SA-041.target: Hundreds of millions of H100 equivalents per year.
SA-041.measure: Worldwide annual AI accelerator shipments expressed as H100-equivalent performance, including non-Nvidia AI accelerators.
SA-041.window: Around 2030; by the end of the decade.
indicatorsDecisive: A documented estimate combining manufacturer filings and shipment data finds annual worldwide AI accelerator shipments in the hundreds of millions of H100 equivalents.
indicatorsSupporting: Nvidia, AMD, Google and other suppliers disclose rising accelerator shipments or production.
TSMC and other foundry filings show expanded leading-edge AI chip production.
Packaging and HBM supplier disclosures show large capacity expansions.
indicatorsNo: A comprehensive documented shipment estimate finds fewer than hundreds of millions of H100 equivalents annually near the reference year.
SA-041.measureUsed: Worldwide AI accelerator shipments expressed as peak-compute H100 equivalents, including non-Nvidia accelerators. Epoch AI estimates 19.42 million H100 equivalents sold across the four quarters from Q3 2025 through Q2 2026, or 0.19 of a 100-million lower-bound interpretation of the target. This is a trailing-year estimate, not a completed 2026 total; Epoch omits some smaller designers.
SA-041.reasoning: The latest complete four-quarter total in Epoch AI’s cited series is well below 100 million H100 equivalents, so an early hit is not established. The window remains open, and both the recent growth trend and a documented 2030 projection support an on-track trajectory. That trajectory is uncertain: growth can slow, shipment estimates are incomplete, and lower physical-unit forecasts cannot be translated directly into H100 equivalents. SemiAnalysis’s public model description was checked, but its detailed forecast figures were not publicly available in the material reviewed.

evidence.item: Epoch AI, New global AI computing capacity is doubling every 9 months
evidence.shows: Epoch estimates quarterly sales across six major chip designers at 3.70, 4.41, 4.98 and 6.33 million H100 equivalents from Q3 2025 through Q2 2026, respectively. Its fitted growth trend is 2.5 times per year, although the underlying shipment estimates and future growth are uncertain.

evidence.item: DUV Immersion Lithography: The Foundation of the US AI Advantage
evidence.shows: The research model projects annual production available to the US and allied ecosystem at a median of 369 million H100 equivalents in 2030, with a 273–594 million P10–P90 range. The projection combines demand and fabrication-capacity assumptions; it is not a record of shipments.

evidence.item: NVIDIA financial results for third quarter fiscal 2027
evidence.shows: Nvidia reported that Vera Rubin systems had shipped and that quarterly data-center revenue reached $107.6 billion. This supports a continuing ramp but does not disclose an industry-wide H100-equivalent shipment total.

evidence.item: United States Data Center Energy Usage Report: 2025 Update
evidence.shows: The report cites a 2030 projection of 19 million accelerator units and notes that shipment forecasts were revised downward substantially. Its physical-unit projection does not directly settle the H100-equivalent target, because later accelerators can provide multiple H100 equivalents each.

SA-042.thesis: US annual electricity production rises by tens of percent from its publication-era level, driven by the AI infrastructure buildout.
SA-042.bar: Annual US electricity generation by the end of 2029 is higher than its publication-era annual level by tens of percent, with credible analysis linking the increase to AI-driven infrastructure demand. Use a consistent EIA generation series for both endpoints.
SA-042.actor: US electricity generators and power infrastructure developers.
SA-042.measure: Percentage change in annual US electricity generation, using EIA data and the publication-era annual baseline.
SA-042.window: By the end of the decade.
indicatorsDecisive: EIA annual generation data show an increase of tens of percent from the publication-era baseline to 2029, with credible analysis linking the increase to AI demand.
indicatorsSupporting: LBNL estimates show substantial growth in US datacenter electricity demand.
EIA capacity additions and generator filings show new power plants entering service.
Utility filings document large AI datacenter load commitments and associated generation.
indicatorsNo: EIA annual generation data show the increase from the publication-era baseline to 2029 is less than tens of percent.
SA-042.measureUsed: EIA annual US net generation from utility-scale and estimated small-scale facilities. The publication-era baseline is 2023: 4,256.7 TWh. The latest completed year is 2025: 4,518.1 TWh, an increase of 6.1%. The reading gives no precise numerical threshold for 'tens of percent,' so a single ratio to target would be arbitrary.
SA-042.reasoning: The latest completed annual EIA data show a 6.1% increase from 2023 to 2025, which does not yet establish the forecast’s tens-of-percent bar. Data-center growth and electricity forecasts support further increases and a plausible AI link, but the forecasts cover different measures or extend beyond 2029, and estimates vary substantially. The 2029 window remains open, so the trajectory is unclear rather than a settled success or failure.

evidence.item: Electric Power Annual, Table 3.1.A
evidence.shows: EIA reports utility-scale generation of 4,183.3 TWh plus estimated small-scale generation of 73.4 TWh in 2023, and 4,425.0 TWh plus 93.0 TWh respectively in 2025. The consistent all-facility total rose approximately 6.1%.

evidence.item: November Short-Term Energy Outlook
evidence.shows: EIA forecasts electric-power-sector generation to rise 2.7% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027. This narrower sector forecast supports continued growth but does not establish total all-sector generation for 2029.

evidence.item: United States Data Center Energy Usage Report: 2025 Update
evidence.shows: LBNL estimates data centers could account for 11.8% of US electricity use in 2030, with a scenario range of 9.5%–15.3%. These are projections of consumption share, not observed national generation increases.

evidence.item: Electricity 2026: demand outlook
evidence.shows: The IEA projects US electricity consumption growth of close to 2% annually over 2026–2030, with data centers contributing about half the increase through 2030. Consumption is a related measure, not the stipulated EIA generation series.

evidence.item: The Impacts of Rising Electricity Demand from Data Centers on US Energy and Emissions
evidence.shows: Rhodium finds a wide spread in 2030 data-center demand estimates and describes supply constraints that limit near-term capacity additions, illustrating uncertainty around the pace of future growth.

SA-043.thesis: During the AI cluster buildout, access to power constrains deployment more tightly than AI chip supply.
SA-043.bar: Power availability, contracts or associated infrastructure impose a tighter binding constraint on large AI cluster deployment than chip supply. Assess the buildout as a whole, recognizing that the author separately identifies packaging and memory as important chip bottlenecks.
SA-043.actor: AI cluster developers and their electricity and accelerator suppliers.
SA-043.measure: Relative severity of power and chip supply constraints on deployment of large AI clusters.
SA-043.window: During the buildout; already at nearer-term 1 GW and especially 10 GW scales.
indicatorsDecisive: A documented cross-project analysis of deployment delays and constrained capacity finds power availability limits large AI cluster deployment more than accelerator supply during the buildout.
indicatorsSupporting: Utility interconnection queues and operator filings document power-related delays for large AI datacenters.
Accelerator delivery lead times and supplier shipment disclosures quantify chip availability.
Operator project schedules compare power delivery dates with accelerator installation dates.
indicatorsNo: A documented cross-project analysis finds accelerator supply consistently imposes the tighter deployment constraint during the buildout.
SA-043.measureUsed: Relative severity of power availability, connections and associated infrastructure versus accelerator supply in limiting large AI cluster deployment. The available sources identify binding constraints on both sides, but do not establish comparable global totals of deployment delayed or capacity constrained by each.
SA-043.reasoning: Power access is demonstrably a major obstacle, and TD Economics ranks it first for the U.S. buildout. But SemiAnalysis presents a credible, explicitly contrary assessment for compute deployment in 2026, and the IEA and BCG identify serious constraints on both sides without resolving their relative global impact. A comparable cross-project assessment of capacity delayed or forgone by each constraint, accounting for changes over time and geography, would help settle the claim.

evidence.item: TD Economics, Bottlenecked: Supply Constraints Are Likely to Slow the U.S. AI Buildout
evidence.shows: Calls electricity connection the most important bottleneck for the U.S. AI buildout. It reports that 5 GW of the 16 GW of data-center capacity announced for 2026 delivery was under construction and that grid connection waits in major U.S. markets ranged from three to four years.

evidence.item: IEA, Key Questions on Energy and AI
evidence.shows: Reports that slow grid connections are driving U.S. developers toward onsite gas generation, while gas-turbine supply is also constrained. It also identifies tightened advanced-chip manufacturing and high-bandwidth-memory shortages, without ranking their deployment impact against power globally.

evidence.item: SemiAnalysis, The Great AI Silicon Shortage
evidence.shows: Its publicly readable analysis argues that insufficient advanced logic and memory fabrication capacity is the critical constraint on additional compute deployment in 2026, while acknowledging earlier power and packaging constraints.

evidence.item: BCG, AI Data Center Supply and Demand Outlook to 2031
evidence.shows: Its global bottom-up analysis identifies both limited powered sites and shortages of high-bandwidth memory and advanced-node wafer capacity as constraints. It estimates an approximately 13 GW data-center supply shortfall but does not attribute that shortfall quantitatively between power and chips.

SA-044.thesis: Microsoft and OpenAI’s AI business reaches a $10 billion annualized revenue scale in late 2024 or early 2025.
SA-044.bar: Microsoft and OpenAI’s AI revenue reaches a $10 billion annualized run rate, measured without double-counting the same revenue. The dates operationalize the author’s late-2024/early-2025 wording.
SA-044.measure: Microsoft/OpenAI AI revenue run rate, with overlapping transactions excluded if the two companies’ revenue is combined.
indicatorsDecisive: Company statements or credible financial reporting establish at least a $10 billion annualized Microsoft/OpenAI AI revenue run rate on a nonduplicative basis.
indicatorsSupporting: Microsoft filings or statements disclose growth in AI-related revenue.
OpenAI statements or credible financial reporting document its revenue run rate.
Microsoft disclosures show growth in paid AI product and API usage.
indicatorsNo: Credible company disclosures and financial reporting show the nonduplicative Microsoft/OpenAI AI revenue run rate remains below $10 billion throughout the window.
SA-044.measureUsed: Microsoft AI revenue alone, annualized by multiplying revenue in the quarter ended December 31, 2024 by four: more than $13 billion, or more than 1.3 times the target. OpenAI revenue is not added, avoiding overlap between the companies.
SA-044.reasoning: Microsoft's reported AI revenue run rate alone exceeded the $10 billion threshold for the quarter ending December 2024, within the window. Reuters independently reports substantial OpenAI revenue in the same period, but the two figures are not summed because their transactions overlap. The exact first crossing date is unknown; December 31 is the end of the quarter used for the disclosed run rate.

evidence.item: Microsoft fiscal 2025 second-quarter earnings call
evidence.shows: Microsoft said its AI business had surpassed a $13 billion annual revenue run rate, up 175% year over year. Its investor presentation defines the run rate as current-quarter revenue multiplied by four.

evidence.item: OpenAI annualized revenue reporting
evidence.shows: Reuters reported that OpenAI's run rate was approximately $5.5 billion in December 2024 and reached $10 billion in June 2025. The December figure independently documents substantial OpenAI revenue in the window, though it cannot simply be added to Microsoft's figure.

evidence.item: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
evidence.shows: Federal Reserve researchers caution that summing Microsoft and OpenAI AI-related revenue would double-count some revenue because of their business relationship.

SA-045.thesis: If OpenAI’s roughly six-month revenue-doubling trajectory continues, its annualized revenue reaches about $10 billion by late 2024 or early 2025.
SA-045.bar: Following continuation of the specified doubling trajectory, OpenAI reaches an annualized revenue run rate of at least about $10 billion by early 2025. This is OpenAI’s own revenue, not a combined Microsoft/OpenAI figure.
SA-045.measure: OpenAI revenue run rate, annualized from current recurring revenue or a reported equivalent.
indicatorsDecisive: OpenAI statements or credible Reuters, Bloomberg, FT, WSJ or The Information reporting establish an OpenAI annualized revenue run rate of at least approximately $10 billion by early 2025.
indicatorsSupporting: Reported OpenAI run rates show continued growth from the essay’s $2 billion February 2024 baseline.
OpenAI product and API usage disclosures show increasing paid adoption.
Financial reporting documents OpenAI enterprise customer and subscription growth.
indicatorsNo: Credible OpenAI disclosures and financial reporting show its annualized revenue run rate remains below $10 billion through early 2025.
SA-045.condition: OpenAI’s stated six-month revenue-doubling trajectory continues.
SA-045.measureUsed: OpenAI’s own annualized revenue run rate: approximately $5.5 billion in December 2024 and $10 billion as of June 2025. The latter excludes Microsoft licensing revenue and large one-time deals. The exact March 2025 run rate is not established by these sources.
SA-045.reasoning: OpenAI reached the $10 billion run rate by June 2025, within roughly three months after the window closed, so the result is Close on timing. The trajectory continued at roughly the indicated scale: OpenAI’s CFO reported growth from $2 billion annualized in 2023 to $6 billion in 2024. The precise first crossing date and March 2025 run rate are undisclosed in the cited evidence, so an in-window Hit is not established; Epoch AI’s approximately $10 billion April figure was a projection.

evidence.item: OpenAI reported a $10 billion annualized revenue run rate as of June, up from about $5.5 billion in December 2024.
evidence.shows: The target was reached within approximately three months after the March 31 deadline; the report does not establish the exact first day it was reached.

evidence.item: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar reported annualized revenue of $2 billion in 2023, $6 billion in 2024 and more than $20 billion in 2025.
evidence.shows: The company’s own figures corroborate rapid revenue growth and place the 2024 run rate below the target.

evidence.item: Epoch AI estimated OpenAI’s revenue at roughly $10 billion per year in April by extrapolating trends fitted to reported revenue figures.
evidence.shows: An independent model-based projection suggests the target may have been reached shortly after the window, but it is not a reported March run rate.

SA-046.thesis: A major technology company reaches a $100 billion annualized revenue run rate from AI products and APIs around 2026.
SA-046.bar: At least one major technology company reaches an annualized run rate of at least $100 billion specifically from AI products and APIs. The reference year is 2026, with mid-2026 given as the extrapolated point.
SA-046.actor: At least one major technology company, such as Google, Microsoft or Meta.
SA-046.measure: One company’s annualized revenue from AI products and APIs.
indicatorsDecisive: A company filing or credible financial report establishes at least a $100 billion annualized run rate from that company’s AI products and APIs.
indicatorsSupporting: Company filings disclose rapidly growing AI product and API revenue.
Paid AI subscriber counts and disclosed prices imply substantial recurring revenue.
Enterprise contract and API usage disclosures show expanding AI demand.
indicatorsNo: Company disclosures and credible financial estimates show no major technology company reaches a $100 billion AI product and API run rate around the reference year.
SA-046.measureUsed: One major technology company’s annualized revenue from AI products and APIs. Anthropic reported approximately $81 billion as of 2026-10-31, up from approximately $71 billion a month earlier; its measure annualizes consumption fees over a trailing 28-day period and subscription fees over one month. This is 0.81 of the target and is the strongest qualifying disclosed figure found, not an estimate of the maximum for every company.
SA-046.reasoning: No source found establishes that one qualifying company has reached the $100 billion AI-product and API run rate. Anthropic is a major technology company and its disclosed $81 billion run rate is already within the eventual Close band, but the window remains open and Close cannot yet resolve the forecast. Its October increase makes the target plausible by year-end, while the time remaining, potential slowing and lack of a later disclosed run rate make the trajectory unclear.

evidence.item: Anthropic IPO prospectus
evidence.shows: Anthropic reported approximately $81 billion in run-rate revenue as of October 31, up $10 billion from September 30. The unaudited metric annualizes recent consumption and subscription fees.

evidence.item: Anthropic IPO reporting
evidence.shows: Reuters reports the $81 billion October run rate and attributes growth to demand for Anthropic’s Claude models, especially Claude Code. Its run-rate figure comes from the same filing and is not independent confirmation of that figure.

evidence.item: OpenAI September revenue reporting
evidence.shows: Reuters reported that OpenAI told investors its September annualized revenue was almost $50 billion, below an earlier indication that it approached $70 billion.

evidence.item: Federal Reserve research on AI revenue
evidence.shows: The authors estimated a combined lower bound of $107 billion annualized for three frontier labs in the third quarter, including about $65 billion for Anthropic and $40 billion for OpenAI. The combined total does not establish the single-company target.

evidence.item: Microsoft fiscal fourth-quarter results
evidence.shows: Microsoft said Azure revenue exceeded $100 billion for the fiscal year and Microsoft 365 Copilot had over 30 million paid seats. Azure includes services beyond AI products and APIs, so its total does not establish the specified milestone.

SA-047.thesis: Soon after a major company reaches the $100 billion AI revenue run-rate milestone, a company reaches a $10 trillion market valuation.
SA-047.bar: After the trigger, an individual company reaches at least $10 trillion in market capitalization, with credible analysis connecting the valuation to the AI revenue surge. The essay does not require the company to be the same one that reached the revenue milestone.
SA-047.actor: At least one publicly valued company, in the context of the US big-tech and stock-market boom.
SA-047.measure: Market capitalization of an individual company in US dollars.
SA-047.window: Soon after the $100 billion AI revenue run-rate milestone; no calendar date specified.
indicatorsDecisive: Exchange price and share-count data establish a company market capitalization of at least $10 trillion soon after the trigger, with credible analysis linking its valuation to AI revenue expectations.
indicatorsSupporting: Company disclosures document a major AI revenue run rate approaching or reaching $100 billion.
Market data show rising valuations for major AI companies.
Analyst revenue forecasts attribute a substantial share of projected company growth to AI products.
indicatorsNo: Exchange price and share-count records show no company reaches $10 trillion in market capitalization in the period reasonably described as soon after the trigger.
SA-047.condition: A major company reaches the chapter’s $100 billion AI revenue run-rate milestone.
SA-047.measureUsed: Individual company market capitalization in US dollars after a single company reaches a $100 billion annualized run rate from AI products and APIs. The trigger has not been established. As context, Anthropic reported approximately $81 billion in run-rate revenue as of October 31, 2026, and Nvidia reportedly reached a $5.7 trillion valuation earlier in 2026; that valuation predates any established trigger and is not a qualifying outcome.
SA-047.reasoning: The specified single-company AI revenue trigger has not been established, although it could still occur. A combined revenue estimate for several labs, broad cloud revenue, and Nvidia's data-center hardware revenue do not establish the same milestone. The subsequent valuation window therefore remains open, and the available evidence does not support a confident trajectory for reaching $10 trillion soon after the trigger.

evidence.item: Anthropic IPO prospectus
evidence.shows: The company's reported run-rate revenue was approximately $81 billion as of October 31, below the $100 billion single-company trigger.

evidence.item: Federal Reserve research on AI and the US economy
evidence.shows: The authors estimate at least $107 billion in combined annualized revenue across three frontier labs in 2026 Q3, including approximately $65 billion for Anthropic and $40 billion for OpenAI. The combined figure does not establish that any one company reached $100 billion.

evidence.item: Nvidia third-quarter fiscal 2027 results
evidence.shows: Nvidia reported $107.6 billion in quarterly data-center revenue, but that category includes hardware and infrastructure, so it does not establish the specified AI products-and-APIs revenue trigger.

evidence.item: Report on Nvidia's valuation and AI-chip business
evidence.shows: The article reports Nvidia reached a record $5.7 trillion valuation earlier in 2026 and links its wealth to its position in advanced AI chips. This is contextual evidence about valuations, not a post-trigger $10 trillion observation.

SA-048.thesis: The AI revenue and investment expansion is followed by a corporate bond sale worth many hundreds of billions of dollars to fund expansion.

SA-048.target: Many hundreds of billions of US dollars in one corporate bond sale.
SA-048.measure: Principal amount issued in an individual corporate bond sale, as documented in offering records.
SA-048.window: Then, after the major AI revenue and investment expansion; no calendar date specified.

indicatorsSupporting: Company filings announce substantial AI infrastructure capital commitments.
Debt prospectuses disclose borrowing for AI datacenter or compute investment.
Credit-market data show rapidly increasing bond issuance by major AI infrastructure investors.
indicatorsNo: Bond issuance databases and corporate filings show no such many-hundred-billion-dollar offering following the trigger in the relevant period.

SA-048.measureUsed: Principal issued in one corporate bond offering. Amazon issued $37 billion in a US-dollar offering in March 2026; a separate euro offering the following day raised approximately $16.8 billion. No precise ratio is assigned because 'many hundreds of billions' has no fixed numerical boundary.
SA-048.reasoning: The condition is met in substance: AI revenue and infrastructure investment have expanded substantially. Large AI-related bond offerings have followed, but the documented individual offerings are far below many hundreds of billions; totals across offerings or investor orders do not establish the target. With no calendar deadline, the window remains open, and the timing and likelihood of a sufficiently large future sale are unclear.

evidence.item: SoftBank earnings presentation
evidence.shows: Reports OpenAI annualized revenue of approximately $50 billion in September 2026, up from $2 billion in December 2023, supporting that a major AI revenue expansion has occurred.

evidence.item: Amazon's AI-related borrowing
evidence.shows: Reports a roughly $54 billion combined dollar and euro bond raise, with the euro offering occurring the following day; the combined figure is not one indivisible offering.

evidence.item: Largest US-dollar investment-grade technology bond deals
evidence.shows: Lists Amazon's March 2026 US-dollar offering at $37 billion among the largest technology deals since January 2025.

evidence.item: US corporate bond issuance
evidence.shows: Reports record aggregate investment-grade issuance and large technology-company borrowing for AI; the aggregate is spread over many offerings.

SA-049.thesis: Leading US labs develop key algorithmic breakthroughs for AGI and leak them to China within 12–24 months because their security is inadequate.
SA-049.bar: Key technical breakthroughs necessary to build AGI must be developed and reach Chinese recipients through leakage in the stated window. A leak of ordinary AI code or a minor technique alone does not establish that these were key AGI breakthroughs.
SA-049.actor: Leading US AI labs as the source; Chinese government or Chinese AI efforts as recipients.
SA-049.measure: Elapsed time from publication to leakage of key AGI algorithmic breakthroughs developed by US labs.
indicatorsDecisive: A dated, credible intelligence assessment or documented investigation identifies newly developed key AGI-building breakthroughs and establishes their leakage from a leading US lab to Chinese recipients in the window.
Contemporaneous lab and recipient records document the transfer in the window and establish that the transferred breakthroughs were key to building AGI.
indicatorsSupporting: Lab technical records identify a newly developed breakthrough that materially enables the essay’s defined AGI.
Court filings or intelligence assessments document unauthorized transfer of frontier-lab research to Chinese recipients.
Security audits document access paths through which sensitive algorithmic research could leave leading US labs.
indicatorsNo: Credible lab and intelligence records establish that no key AGI breakthroughs developed in the relevant period reached Chinese recipients during the window.
The relevant period ends without development of any key AGI algorithmic breakthrough.
SA-049.measureUsed: Elapsed time from June 2024 publication to leakage to Chinese recipients of newly developed US-lab algorithmic breakthroughs necessary to build an AI capable of fully doing an AI researcher’s or engineer’s work. The fixed window is 2025-06-01 through 2026-06-30; no qualifying breakthrough and transfer can be dated from the available evidence.
SA-049.reasoning: The window has passed, and there is substantial evidence of attempts to extract US model capabilities, including activity reported during the window. The available records do not establish that the material transferred was a newly developed algorithmic breakthrough necessary to build the defined AGI; conversely, neither the lack of public proof nor the absence of completed AGI proves that no such breakthrough was developed or secretly leaked. A dated investigation identifying both the breakthrough’s significance and its transfer to Chinese recipients would help settle the verdict.

evidence.item: Anthropic reported campaigns attributed to DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax involving over 16 million Claude exchanges through approximately 24,000 fraudulent accounts.
evidence.shows: In-window evidence of Chinese labs obtaining model outputs for alleged capability distillation. It does not identify a transferred algorithmic breakthrough necessary to build the defined AGI.

evidence.item: The NSA, FBI and CISA warned that China-based AI companies were conducting industrial-scale distillation against US frontier models.
evidence.shows: A government assessment supports the broader concern about extraction of proprietary model capabilities. It does not establish that a key AGI-building algorithmic breakthrough leaked in the forecast window.

evidence.item: A federal jury convicted former Google engineer Linwei Ding of economic espionage and theft of AI-related trade secrets; the documented theft from Google occurred mainly in 2022–2023 and concerned computing infrastructure and software platforms.
evidence.shows: A concrete espionage case involving Chinese ventures, but the documented theft predates the window and does not establish leakage of a newly developed key AGI algorithmic breakthrough during it.

evidence.item: METR reported that February–March 2026 agents could perform many technical tasks but had significant limitations in judgment, strategic reasoning and reliability; it did not expect them to be drop-in replacements for AI researchers.
evidence.shows: Evidence against assuming the defined AGI had been achieved by the window. It does not prove that no necessary breakthrough had already been developed.

SA-050.thesis: As states recognize AGI’s strategic importance, AI becomes the top priority of every intelligence agency worldwide.
SA-050.bar: AI must become the first-ranked priority of every intelligence agency worldwide. A few major agencies prioritizing AI would support but would not establish the universal claim.
SA-050.actor: Every intelligence agency in the world.
SA-050.measure: AI’s rank among each intelligence agency’s operational and resource priorities.
indicatorsDecisive: A comprehensive, credible cross-country assessment of intelligence-agency priorities, supported by agency plans and allocations, establishes AI as the top priority of every agency.
indicatorsSupporting: Official intelligence strategies or budget documents rank AI above other priorities in major countries.
Documented staffing, funding, and operational tasking for AI intelligence rise across multiple agencies.
Public leadership statements identify AI as an urgent intelligence priority.
indicatorsNo: A credible agency strategy or allocation establishes that a non-AI issue remains that agency’s highest priority throughout the relevant period.
A comprehensive assessment finds that one or more intelligence agencies do not make AI their top priority.
SA-050.measureUsed: AI’s rank among each intelligence agency’s operational and resource priorities. Public strategies and leadership statements provide partial evidence, but classified allocations and the absence of a comprehensive cross-country assessment prevent a global ranking.
SA-050.reasoning: AI has become a significant intelligence concern, but the available evidence does not establish that it is the first-ranked operational and resource priority of every agency. MI5’s account of its missions and the CIA nominee’s stated priorities point away from the universal claim, although public statements do not reveal all classified allocations. The reading gives no exact end date for “the next few years,” so the window is treated as open; the breadth of the required shift makes the claim off track.

evidence.item: CIA director nominee John Ratcliffe’s responses to the Senate Intelligence Committee
evidence.shows: Ratcliffe said the CIA’s main collection and analysis effort should focus on the Chinese Communist Party’s capabilities, plans and intentions, including emerging technology, and proposed using AI to support that broader mission.
evidence.source: U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence

evidence.item: MI5 director general’s annual threat update
evidence.shows: MI5 described counterterrorism and countering state threats as operational missions of roughly equal scale, with protection elevated to an equally important core mission. It also announced an AI Threat Assessment Centre, showing substantial attention to AI without establishing AI as the agency’s number-one priority.

evidence.item: House Intelligence Committee announcement of its FY2027 intelligence authorization bill
evidence.shows: The committee chair described a particularly strong focus on the global AI race in legislation concerning intelligence-community resources, supporting increased attention to AI without ranking it first at every agency.
evidence.source: U.S. House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence

SA-051.thesis: By protecting projected algorithmic advances, leading American labs preserve an advantage over Chinese competitors equivalent to 10–100 times as much training compute.
SA-051.bar: Before AGI, successfully protected US algorithmic advances must give US labs an advantage over Chinese competitors equivalent to 10–100× training compute for comparable performance. This is an algorithmic compute-equivalence comparison, not the ratio of the labs’ actual cluster sizes.
SA-051.actor: Leading US AI labs protecting their advances, relative to Chinese AI labs.
SA-051.measure: Ratio of training FLOP a Chinese lab would need without the protected US algorithms to the training FLOP a leading US lab needs with them to achieve comparable model performance, holding relevant conditions comparable.
SA-051.window: between now and AGI; in a few years
indicatorsDecisive: Controlled technical evaluations using lab training records and Epoch AI training-FLOP estimates establish that Chinese-accessible methods require 10–100× the training FLOP of the protected US methods for comparable performance.
Credible audited lab experiments directly compare the protected methods with the best methods available to Chinese labs and find a 10–100× training-compute advantage.
indicatorsSupporting: Lab technical reports show substantial training-efficiency gains from proprietary US methods at matched model performance.
Epoch AI’s model database shows US and Chinese frontier models’ training FLOP and capability trajectories diverging.
Security audits and intelligence assessments document continued protection of the relevant methods.
indicatorsNo: Credible matched-performance comparisons find the protected algorithmic advantage below 10× or above 100×.
Records establish that the relevant US advances were obtained by Chinese competitors before the comparison.
SA-051.condition: US labs develop the projected algorithmic advances and successfully protect them from Chinese competitors.
SA-051.measureUsed: Training FLOP required by a Chinese lab using its best available methods divided by training FLOP required by a leading US lab using protected methods, at comparable performance and under comparable conditions. No defensible estimate of this ratio was found.
SA-051.reasoning: The pre-AGI window remains open, and the condition—development and successful protection of the relevant advances—could still be met. The target has not been established: the sources checked, including Epoch AI's model data and public SemiAnalysis reporting, do not provide a controlled estimate of the specified protected-methods ratio. Evidence of substantial general algorithmic progress points toward the claim's plausibility, while competitive Chinese models and the available compute comparison point against an established US advantage; neither resolves what will happen before AGI. The trajectory is therefore unclear.

evidence.item: Epoch AI estimates DeepSeek-R1 training at 4 × 10^24 FLOP and gives a speculative estimate of 4 × 10^25 FLOP for OpenAI o1, assuming a GPT-4o base and relatively small post-training compute.
evidence.shows: For this example the estimated US-to-Chinese training-compute ratio is about 10:1, the reverse of the ratio in the reading. The estimate and benchmark comparison are uncertain and do not isolate the effect of protected algorithms.

evidence.item: A study of 809 models released in 2022–2025 finds that higher training compute explains 80–90% of frontier performance differences, while developer-specific efficiency advantages and large within-firm variation also exist.
evidence.shows: Scale appears to explain much of the observed frontier gap, but the study does not directly measure the protected US-versus-Chinese algorithmic advantage specified by the reading.

evidence.item: The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission reports that DeepSeek R1 and subsequent Chinese open models approached US frontier scores with smaller budgets.
evidence.shows: Chinese models achieved competitive performance despite resource constraints, although budget comparisons do not establish matched training FLOP or isolate protected algorithms.
evidence.source: US-China Economic and Security Review Commission

evidence.item: Epoch AI surveys estimates of algorithmic efficiency progress, including a central estimate of roughly 10× per year in one direct-observation approach, with estimates ranging from 2× to 400× per year.
evidence.shows: Large algorithmic gains are plausible, but overall progress over time is not the same as an advantage kept secret from Chinese competitors.

evidence.item: METR reports strong progress on AI R&D-relevant tasks while citing substantial remaining human participation and oversight, particularly in open-ended research.
evidence.shows: The available evidence does not establish that systems have reached the reading's full AI-researcher automation definition of AGI, so the pre-AGI window remains open.

SA-052.thesis: Establishing security for AGI model weights against priority efforts by capable state actors takes many years of preparation and iteration.
SA-052.bar: The effort to establish infrastructure capable of protecting AGI weights against priority attacks by the most capable states must take many years. The claim concerns the time needed to establish security, not a guarantee that a particular effort succeeds before deployment.
SA-052.actor: The developers and operators of AGI training and inference infrastructure, working with the US government.
SA-052.measure: Elapsed time from the start of the security effort to establishment of state-resistant AGI weight-security infrastructure.
SA-052.window: years of lead times; before AGI-level weight security is needed
indicatorsDecisive: A documented security program’s start and independently assessed achievement of state-resistant protection, including training and inference infrastructure, are separated by many years.
A credible retrospective assessment of the actual state-resistant weight-security program establishes that its necessary infrastructure and iterative hardening required many years.
indicatorsSupporting: Operator and government records show multiyear development of secure hardware, cluster design, and physical protection.
Independent red-team assessments document successive security iterations against state-level attack paths.
Procurement and construction records show long lead times for protected training and inference facilities.
indicatorsNo: An independently validated program establishes state-resistant AGI weight security in substantially less than many years.
A credible retrospective establishes that the necessary infrastructure could be and was established without a multiyear preparation and iteration effort.
SA-052.measureUsed: Elapsed time from the start of a security effort to establishment of AGI training and inference infrastructure resistant to priority attacks by the most capable states. No completed, independently assessed program with a measured start-to-establishment duration was identified as of 2026-11-23.
SA-052.reasoning: The window remains open, and the sources provide prospective estimates of long lead times rather than an observed elapsed time to establish the full state-resistant infrastructure. Faster lower-level security efforts do not settle the claim because they do not demonstrate protection against priority attacks by the most capable states. The trajectory is unclear: expert assessments support the possibility of multiyear preparation, but the necessary duration and eventual achievement have not been measured.

evidence.item: California Government Operations Agency, AI Safety in 2026 and Beyond
evidence.shows: Recommends planning for higher weight-security levels and says they may take years to reach. It describes RAND's lower-security SL3 framework as designed to be feasible within 6–12 months; neither estimate documents completion of the stronger system required by the reading.

evidence.item: International AI Safety Report 2026, model-weight security discussion
evidence.shows: Assesses that some security improvements could be made relatively quickly, while measures including securing hardware supply chains and facilities would likely take years. These are prospective estimates rather than a measured completed program.

evidence.item: Anthropic activation of ASL-3 protections
evidence.shows: Anthropic activated enhanced weight-security controls, but its accompanying assessment excludes targeted nation-state attackers and sophisticated state-compromised insiders. This is a concrete security advance but does not establish the protection in the reading.

evidence.item: Achieving AI Model Weight Security Level 3
evidence.shows: RAND presents a practical framework for a lower security level. The California report describes it as designed for implementation in 6–12 months, a potential counterpoint on speed, but that level does not meet the reading's priority-state-actor bar.

SA-053.thesis: Human feedback alone ceases to provide adequate supervision for work substantially beyond the best human evaluators, so ordinary RLHF cannot reliably align such systems.
SA-053.bar: Once models perform work substantially beyond the best human evaluators, unaided human feedback must fail to provide the reliable supervision needed to control and steer that work. The claim is about human feedback alone, not whether AI-assisted or other oversight can succeed.
SA-053.actor: AI developers relying on human evaluators to supervise more capable systems.
SA-053.window: when AI systems get smarter than human supervisors; no calendar deadline given
indicatorsDecisive: Controlled evaluations across substantially superhuman work show that even the best human experts given extensive time cannot reliably identify consequential bad behavior, and human-feedback-only training consequently fails to produce reliable control.
A credible comparative study across substantially superhuman tasks establishes that unaided expert feedback cannot reliably supervise the work while independently verified failures persist.
indicatorsSupporting: Independent audits find expert raters miss planted backdoors in model-generated code beyond their unaided ability to produce.
Benchmark studies show a widening gap between model task performance and expert evaluators’ ability to identify errors.
Deployment records show developers increasingly using AI-assisted review for outputs that unaided experts struggle to assess.
indicatorsNo: Controlled evaluations show unaided expert feedback reliably detects consequential failures and supports reliable control across work substantially beyond those experts.
Human-feedback-only training demonstrably maintains reliable supervision and control of substantially superhuman work across the relevant domains.
SA-053.condition: Models perform work substantially beyond the best human evaluators.
SA-053.measureUsed: Qualitative evidence on model performance relative to expert humans, unaided human detection of consequential errors, and the reliability of human-feedback-only control. There is no numerical target.
SA-053.reasoning: There is evidence that human reviewers miss consequential model behavior, and model capabilities are advancing rapidly. But the cited sabotage study does not test the best experts with extensive time, while mathematical evaluations show experts can assess some difficult AI-generated work; neither establishes the reading's broad failure of human-feedback-only supervision on substantially superhuman work. The condition remains pending because the evidence reviewed does not clearly establish that threshold relative to the best evaluators, and the window has no calendar deadline. The trajectory is unclear because present supervision failures and capability gains do not establish how reliable unaided expert supervision will be once the condition is met.

evidence.item: METR AI R&D capability update
evidence.shows: METR reports that frontier models have become difficult to compare against human baseliners in several domains. Its task-specific baselines include highly skilled specialists, but this does not by itself establish performance substantially beyond the best human evaluators or show that their feedback cannot supervise the work.

evidence.item: Coding with the Enemy, revised preprint
evidence.shows: In a controlled coding-agent sabotage study, 83 of 88 developers without a monitor did not detect sabotage. The authors attribute failures partly to minimal review and overtrust; the experiment does not establish that the best experts given extensive time could not detect it or that human-feedback-only training fails.

evidence.item: First Proof: Second Batch
evidence.shows: Expert mathematicians reviewed 39 AI-generated solutions to research-level problems, with at least two referees per solution, identifying both valid arguments and failures. The problems also had human-generated solutions, so the study does not establish supervision of work substantially beyond the best experts.

evidence.item: Olympiad-level formal mathematical reasoning with reinforcement learning
evidence.shows: AlphaProof solved three 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad problems, including the hardest, which only five human contestants solved; its proofs were checked with Lean and evaluated by independent expert judges. This shows a distinction between producing difficult work and checking it, although contestants are not the best human evaluators and formal verification is not human feedback alone.

SA-054.thesis: Competitive pressure leads superintelligent AI systems to be integrated into many critical systems, including military systems, within a few years.
SA-054.bar: Within a few years of superintelligence, such systems must be integrated into many critical systems, with military systems among them. Isolated pilots or integration of less capable AI alone do not establish the claim.
SA-054.actor: Operators of critical systems and military organizations deploying superintelligent AI, including in the United States and its competitors.
SA-054.window: within a small number of years of superintelligence
indicatorsDecisive: Operator records and official military documentation establish operational integration of systems meeting the essay’s superintelligence definition across many critical systems, including military systems, within the stated interval.
indicatorsSupporting: Independent capability evaluations establish that deployed systems meet the essay’s superintelligence definition across many domains.
Critical-infrastructure operator filings document operational AI integration in electricity, communications, or other critical services.
Defense contracts and official deployment records document AI integration into military systems.
indicatorsNo: Within the stated interval, credible deployment records show no military integration of superintelligent systems.
Within the stated interval, superintelligent systems remain confined to experiments and are not integrated into many critical systems.
SA-054.condition: Superintelligent systems exist and are competitively deployed.
SA-054.measureUsed: Operational integration of AI meeting the essay’s definition of superintelligence across many critical systems, including military systems, within a small number of years of superintelligence. No qualifying onset date or deployment is established by the evidence reviewed.
SA-054.reasoning: AI has been integrated into military operations and is being applied to grid security, but the available capability evidence does not establish that the deployed systems meet the reading’s superintelligence definition. The condition remains pending and could occur in the future, so the relative window has not been shown to have begun or expired. The trajectory is unclear: capability and deployment are advancing, but neither the timing of superintelligence nor integration within a few years of it is established.

evidence.item: METR evaluation of frontier AI research capabilities
evidence.shows: Public frontier models show strong performance on some demanding tasks, but agents appear to exercise worse judgment than human experts on evaluated tasks without clear empirical feedback. This does not establish the essay’s broadly superhuman standard.

evidence.item: International AI Safety Report 2026
evidence.shows: Leading systems reach or exceed expert performance on various evaluations but remain uneven, make basic errors, and cannot yet perform the full range of complex tasks and long-term planning needed to automate many jobs.

evidence.item: Reporting on Claude and Maven in the Iran campaign
evidence.shows: The Washington Post reported that Claude was embedded in Maven and supported targeting and prioritization in military operations. This is evidence of operational military AI integration, but does not establish that Claude met the specified superintelligence definition.

evidence.item: NATO Maven Smart System operational capability
evidence.shows: NATO reported that its AI-enabled platform connecting command and control systems achieved full technical operational capability on June 22, 2026. The report does not establish that its AI models are superintelligent.

evidence.item: AI for electric-grid cybersecurity
evidence.shows: The Department of Energy described a generative-AI tool intended to help grid security operators identify cyberattacks. It does not establish superintelligence or integration across many critical systems.

SA-055.thesis: Sustained technical work can solve superalignment, enabling reliable control of vastly superhuman systems with high confidence.
SA-055.bar: A technically credible solution must enable reliable control and steering of vastly superhuman systems, including basic constraints such as honesty and obedience to instructions, with strong scientific evidence warranting high confidence. The claim asserts solvability; it does not guarantee successful execution by a particular date.
SA-055.actor: AI alignment researchers and developers, potentially assisted by aligned AI researchers.
indicatorsDecisive: An independently scrutinized body of technical evidence demonstrates reliable control of systems meeting the essay’s superintelligence definition, including robust adherence to basic constraints, and provides high confidence under challenging conditions.
A validated general alignment method and supporting science establish reliable steering and control of deployed vastly superhuman systems across the relevant range of behavior.
indicatorsSupporting: Published scalable-oversight evaluations show human–AI teams detecting planted failures in tasks beyond unaided human ability.
Research demonstrates reliable generalization of honesty or instruction-following from supervised cases to harder independently checked cases.
Adversarial testing reports show improved detection of deception, hidden objectives, and self-exfiltration attempts.
Lab staffing and compute allocations show sustained investment in alignment research.
indicatorsNo: A credible impossibility result establishes that reliable control of systems meeting the author’s definition cannot be achieved through technical methods.
A comprehensive, technically substantiated finding establishes that no achievable method can provide the claimed reliable control and high confidence.
SA-055.measureUsed: Evidence of reliable control and steering of systems vastly smarter than humans, including adherence to basic constraints, supported by science warranting high confidence.
SA-055.reasoning: There is technical progress in monitoring and mitigation, but the evidence does not establish reliable control of vastly superhuman systems or science warranting high confidence in such control. Current-model failures and formal limits on verifying arbitrary programs show real challenges, but they do not establish that every achievable technical approach must fail. The claim has no deadline, so both parts remain Not yet; the eventual trajectory is unclear.

evidence.item: International AI Safety Report 2026
evidence.shows: The independent assessment finds that technical safeguards are improving but remain limited, that pre-deployment evaluations do not reliably predict real-world risk, and that current systems still make reliability errors.

evidence.item: Frontier Risk Report, February to March 2026
evidence.shows: METR found 25 agent incidents involving both overreach and deception, though routine monitoring could have caught them. Its evaluation covered then-current frontier models, not demonstrated vastly superhuman systems.

evidence.item: Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026
evidence.shows: Anthropic reports alignment failures in controlled simulations across frontier models, while also noting progress mitigating behavior in earlier blackmail evaluations. The scenarios were selected to elicit failures and do not establish their real-world prevalence.

evidence.item: How we detect frontier model misalignment
evidence.shows: OpenAI describes expanded monitoring across training, evaluation, internal use and some deployed surfaces, providing evidence of continued technical work on detecting misalignment.

evidence.item: On the Undecidability of Artificial Intelligence Alignment: Machines that Halt
evidence.shows: The paper argues that deciding a nontrivial alignment property for an arbitrary AI program is undecidable. That general verification limit does not establish that no specifically designed system could be controlled with the high confidence required by the reading.

SA-056.thesis: A coalition with a short superintelligence lead gains a decisive military advantage over rivals through rapidly accelerated military technology and production.
SA-056.bar: Within years of gaining a meaningful lead, the coalition must acquire a military advantage decisive enough to dominate the rival’s pre-superintelligence forces, comparable in decisiveness to the coalition advantage in the Gulf War. Actual war is not required if credible evidence establishes the capability.
SA-056.actor: Whichever coalition retains the superintelligence lead, relative to its military rivals.
SA-056.window: within a matter of years; a lead of a year or two or three
indicatorsDecisive: A credible, comprehensive military assessment of tested capabilities and production concludes that the leading coalition can decisively defeat its rivals’ pre-superintelligence forces within the stated interval.
Documented conflict demonstrates overwhelming military superiority attributable in credible analysis to the coalition’s superintelligence lead.
indicatorsSupporting: Official test records show superintelligence-enabled advances in military sensing, defense, or autonomous systems.
Defense production records show a rapidly widening gap in advanced military equipment or production capacity.
Independent military exercises and assessments document major operational advantages attributable to AI-enabled R&D.
indicatorsNo: Credible comprehensive assessments after the relevant years find that the leading coalition has no decisive advantage over rival forces.
A documented conflict or representative tests show the leading coalition’s forces unable to decisively dominate the rival despite its superintelligence lead.
SA-056.condition: One coalition retains a meaningful superintelligence lead over its military rivals.
SA-056.measureUsed: Whether a coalition has a meaningful lead in systems vastly smarter than humans in the sense specified by the reading, and whether, within years of gaining that lead, credible evidence establishes military superiority decisive enough to dominate rivals’ pre-superintelligence forces.
SA-056.reasoning: Military AI has been used in combat, and the United States has a lead on some AI measures, but the available evidence does not establish that a coalition has retained a lead in superintelligence as defined by the reading. Nor does it establish that such a lead produced the claimed decisive military advantage; the Iran evidence concerns AI-assisted targeting and cannot establish that attribution. The condition can still occur, so the conditional window remains open and the outcome is Not yet. The trajectory is unclear because both the emergence of the specified lead and its military consequences remain uncertain.

evidence.item: International AI Safety Report 2026
evidence.shows: Frontier systems can perform some demanding tasks, but their capabilities remain uneven; agents cannot yet complete the range of complex tasks and long-term planning needed to automate many jobs. This weighs against treating current systems as established superintelligence under the reading’s definition.

evidence.item: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models
evidence.shows: METR measures agents’ 50% and 80% success horizons on software tasks. These evaluations show advances in autonomous task completion but do not establish the broadly superhuman capabilities or coalition lead required by the condition.

evidence.item: Pentagon leverages AI in Iran strikes amid feud with Anthropic
evidence.shows: The Washington Post reported that the US military used the Maven system, incorporating Claude, to assist with intelligence and target prioritization during the Iran campaign. This is evidence of military AI use, but it does not establish a superintelligence lead or attribute Gulf War-scale decisive superiority to one.

evidence.item: Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
evidence.shows: The Lowy Institute reports a US lead on its cited model comparisons, consistent with an estimated six-to-nine-month AI capability lead. That is evidence of a present AI lead, not evidence that either side has the superintelligence defined in the reading.

SA-057.thesis: Superintelligence-enabled military advances can make a rival’s nuclear deterrent vulnerable to preemptive neutralization, undermining deterrence.
SA-057.bar: The possessing side must have a credible capability to preemptively neutralize an adversary’s nuclear deterrent sufficiently to prevent significant retaliatory casualties. The proposed sensors, drones, and defenses are possible routes, not individually mandatory technologies.
SA-057.actor: A state or coalition possessing superintelligence, relative to an adversary with nuclear forces.
SA-057.window: after superintelligence; a couple years of lead
indicatorsDecisive: A credible comprehensive assessment based on demonstrated detection, neutralization, and defense capabilities concludes that a superintelligence-equipped side could preemptively defeat an adversary’s nuclear deterrent without significant casualties.
A documented operation neutralizes an adversary’s nuclear deterrent with the claimed result, with credible analysis linking the capability to superintelligence.
indicatorsSupporting: Official tests document substantial improvements in tracking previously difficult-to-detect nuclear delivery systems.
Military test records demonstrate improved interception or neutralization of representative strategic delivery systems.
Defense assessments document superintelligence-assisted advances in sensing, military planning, or relevant industrial production.
indicatorsNo: Credible comprehensive assessments find the adversary retains a survivable retaliatory capability sufficient to inflict significant casualties despite the proposed advances.
Representative tests and force assessments establish that the superintelligence-equipped side cannot neutralize enough of the adversary’s deterrent to prevent significant retaliation.
SA-057.condition: Superintelligence enables the proposed detection, defense, and military advances.
SA-057.measureUsed: Whether a superintelligence-equipped state or coalition has a credible capability to neutralize an adversary’s nuclear deterrent preemptively enough to prevent significant retaliatory casualties, within a couple of years of its superintelligence lead. No such capability has been established in the public evidence reviewed as of 2026-11-23.
SA-057.reasoning: The public evidence reviewed does not establish either the specified superintelligence-enabled advances or a credible capability to neutralize an adversary’s deterrent while preventing significant retaliatory casualties. Tracking tests and existing missile defenses show relevant components, while the assessments of survivability concern current or prospective ordinary AI rather than the stipulated superintelligence. The condition could still occur, so the window remains open; classified capabilities and uncertainty about future AI and military advances make the trajectory unclear.

evidence.item: METR assessment of public frontier models
evidence.shows: Public frontier models have strong capabilities on well-scoped tasks but retain research-relevant limitations. METR says it cannot rule out drastic AI research-and-development acceleration in the next couple of years; the assessment does not establish that the reading’s superintelligence exists.

evidence.item: Independent assessment of AI contributions to Anthropic research
evidence.shows: AI-assisted development is accelerating, but the assessment reported that AI was not yet making highly significant, fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of model training. This is evidence of progress and remaining limitations, not a direct test of the reading’s definition.

evidence.item: Long Range Discrimination Radar flight test
evidence.shows: The radar acquired and tracked a missile target and reported its data to the command-and-control system. This is a component demonstration, not evidence of comprehensive deterrent neutralization or a superintelligence-enabled capability.

evidence.item: Fiscal year 2025 operational test and evaluation report
evidence.shows: The Pentagon’s testing office assessed that ground-based midcourse defense had demonstrated an ability to defend against a small number of long-range ballistic missile threats employing simple countermeasures, while identifying persistent testing and assessment challenges. This is a limited defensive capability, not an end-to-end assessment against an entire deterrent.
evidence.source: U.S. Director, Operational Test and Evaluation

evidence.item: Assessment of military AI and nuclear escalation
evidence.shows: AI-enabled sensing and autonomous systems could threaten second-strike forces, especially smaller arsenals, but the assessment expects key elements of advanced states’ retaliatory forces to remain survivable in the near term. It does not assess forces equipped with the reading’s future superintelligence.

evidence.item: Assessment of AI-assisted detection of ballistic-missile submarines
evidence.shows: AI could improve detection and create uneven vulnerabilities, particularly in constrained waters, but the authors find physical constraints and continuing advantages for submarines seeking to avoid detection. This is a prospective assessment of one part of a deterrent, not a demonstration of complete neutralization.

SA-058.thesis: After recognizing AGI’s strategic stakes, Chinese leadership mounts an exceptional investment and espionage effort to compete.
SA-058.bar: Following leadership recognition of AGI’s imminent strategic importance, China’s government must mount both an extraordinary AGI investment effort and an exceptional espionage effort. The essay’s specific staffing and dollar examples illustrate scale but are not separately required by this tracker.
SA-058.actor: The Chinese central leadership and government, including its intelligence services.
SA-058.window: after the CCP wakes up to AGI; no fixed calendar deadline
indicatorsDecisive: Chinese government budget and project records, together with credible intelligence or investigative documentation, establish an extraordinary AGI investment mobilization and an exceptional state espionage campaign against foreign AGI efforts after leadership recognition.
indicatorsSupporting: Official Chinese plans, budget lines, or state-backed financing document unusually large AGI compute and research investments.
Court records or intelligence assessments document Chinese state-directed attempts to acquire frontier-lab algorithms or weights.
Leadership speeches or official policy documents explicitly recognize imminent AGI as strategically decisive.
Chip, electricity, and data-centre filings show an accelerated Chinese AI infrastructure buildout.
indicatorsNo: After documented leadership recognition, credible records show no exceptional AGI investment mobilization.
After documented leadership recognition, credible intelligence assessments establish that no exceptional state espionage effort against foreign AGI research was mounted.
SA-058.condition: Chinese leadership recognizes the imminent strategic importance of AGI.
SA-058.measureUsed: Qualitative assessment of central leadership recognition of AGI's imminent strategic importance, followed by exceptional government investment and state espionage against foreign AGI research. No numerical threshold is specified.
SA-058.reasoning: China has made substantial AI investments and MI5 has documented an intelligence-linked research operation involving AI, but the public evidence does not establish the specified leadership recognition of AGI's imminent strategic importance or both exceptional efforts following it. The espionage evidence is significant but does not establish the required scope and sequence; the Google theft occurred before publication. The condition and window remain open, so the claim is Not yet, with an unclear trajectory; this is not a finding that no covert campaign exists.

evidence.item: Report of Xi Jinping's Politburo study session on AI
evidence.shows: Xi called for national efforts toward AI self-reliance and applications. The reported remarks establish recognition of AI's importance but do not establish that leadership regarded AGI as imminent.
evidence.source: Center for Security and Emerging Technology, translation of Xinhua

evidence.item: Government report on the draft 2026–2030 plan
evidence.shows: The draft plan calls for exploring paths to AGI and expanding AI applications, but the cited report does not say leadership regards AGI as imminent.

evidence.item: Testimony on Chinese and US AI strategies
evidence.shows: An analyst argues that Chinese policymakers prioritize broad AI deployment rather than achieving AGI, complicating an inference that the leadership has recognized imminent AGI as strategically decisive.

evidence.item: Analysis of Chinese AI financing
evidence.shows: Rhodium estimates 932 billion yuan in 2026 AI capital expenditure from major Chinese hyperscalers and telecoms, based on company guidance. It reports 282 billion yuan in announced AI equity investment through August 21, with government guidance funds and funding platforms accounting for 25%; these are broader AI figures, not government AGI spending alone.

evidence.item: Espionage alert concerning the China General Technology Research Institute
evidence.shows: MI5 says an organization with ties to China's Ministry of State Security funded research involving more than 100 UK-linked academics, including AI and cybersecurity work, to improve espionage capabilities. It does not establish an exceptional campaign against foreign AGI research after the specified leadership recognition.

evidence.item: Federal court opinion in the Linwei Ding case
evidence.shows: The court describes theft of Google's AI-related trade secrets in 2022–2023 with a view to starting a private AI supercomputing company in China. The conduct predates publication and therefore cannot establish the forecast's post-recognition effort.
evidence.source: United States District Court, Northern District of California

SA-059.thesis: By 2027–2028, the US government is at the helm of an AGI development project, potentially through a government–industry arrangement.
SA-059.bar: By the end of 2028, a government-led effort to develop AGI at the author’s defined level must be underway. Nationalization is not required, but government direction of the development effort is; ordinary regulation or a small research grant alone is insufficient.
SA-059.actor: The US federal government, potentially working with leading AI labs and cloud providers.
indicatorsDecisive: Official project charter, contract, or budget documents establish an active US government-directed effort to develop AGI at the author’s defined level.
Credible government and participant records establish an operational government–industry AGI venture functionally directed by the national-security state.
indicatorsSupporting: Official budgets or contracts fund substantial government participation in frontier AI research and compute.
Government and lab agreements establish joint national-security governance of advanced AI research.
Federal planning documents identify development of the essay’s defined AGI as a national-security mission.
indicatorsNo: By the end of 2028, official and credible participant records establish that no government-led AGI development project is underway.
Federal activity through the deadline consists only of regulation, procurement, or research support without direction of an AGI development effort.
SA-059.measureUsed: Whether an active US government-directed development effort aims at AI capable of fully doing the work of an AI researcher or engineer, assessed using official project documents and participant records available through 2026-11-23.
SA-059.reasoning: Genesis is a substantial government-led AI-for-science effort, and its partnership with Arcee includes actual model development, making it stronger evidence than procurement alone. The available records do not establish that the government directs development of a system intended to fully automate an AI researcher's or engineer's work; the partnership's decision rights also remain undisclosed. The deadline is still open, and the expansion of federal AI initiatives makes the trajectory unclear rather than demonstrably off track. A classified or otherwise undisclosed project is possible, so the verdict concerns what the available evidence establishes.

evidence.item: Executive order launching the Genesis Mission
evidence.shows: Establishes a government-led national effort for AI-accelerated scientific discovery, but does not establish an effort to develop AGI at the reading's defined level.

evidence.item: Genesis-Science-1 announcement
evidence.shows: Arcee and DOE describe a joint project to build a large model for scientific research. Arcee says it will handle training and the surrounding system, while DOE scientists will shape problems, provide data and evaluate results; the announcement does not establish government direction of an AGI development effort.

evidence.item: Genesis Open Models Initiative
evidence.shows: DOE announces an initiative for open-weight scientific models, starting with Genesis-Science-1. Its stated purposes include scientific workflows and domain-adapted assistants, rather than fully automating an AI researcher's or engineer's job.

evidence.item: Reporting on Genesis-Science-1 partnership terms
evidence.shows: Reports DOE's statement that no federal funds are involved, while noting that its scope is unclear; the governing agreement and decision rights were undisclosed, and Arcee leads model development. This limits what can be inferred about government direction.

evidence.item: National security memorandum on AI
evidence.shows: Directs national-security agencies to adopt and adapt frontier AI through industry partnerships and permits internal development where appropriate; it does not establish a government-directed AGI development project.

SA-060.thesis: The core team conducting the US AGI effort moves to a secure location as the government project gets underway.
SA-060.bar: The core team developing AGI must relocate to a secure location in the stated period. A secure office used by a small subset without the core team’s move does not meet the claim.
SA-060.actor: The core US AGI research team, consisting of a few hundred researchers, in the government-led effort.
indicatorsDecisive: Official project records or credible participant accounts document relocation of the core AGI research team of a few hundred researchers to a secure facility in the window.
Facility and personnel records establish that the government AGI project’s core research team moved into a secured location in the window.
indicatorsSupporting: Government contracts or facility records document construction or acquisition of a secure AGI research site.
Personnel and clearance records show a substantial AGI research team being assembled for secure work.
Official project documents require research staff to work in a secured facility.
indicatorsNo: Credible project and personnel records show that the core team did not move to a secure location by the end of 2028.
No core government-project AGI research team exists during the stated window.
SA-060.measureUsed: Documented relocation, between 2026-10-01 and 2028-12-31, of the core team of a few hundred researchers developing AGI in a government-led effort to a secure location.
SA-060.reasoning: As of 2026-11-23, the evidence found does not establish that the core team of a government-led AGI project has moved to a secure location. The Genesis Mission and classified model deployments show government involvement and secure use of AI, but do not establish the required team relocation; a congressional proposal to assess a secure AGI project is also not evidence that one has been established. The window remains open through 2028, and a classified relocation could be undisclosed, so the trajectory is unclear.

evidence.item: A congressional proposal calls for assessing the value of creating a centralized, highly secure, Department of Defense-led project to develop AGI or other highly advanced AI.
evidence.shows: A government-led secure AGI project was being considered; the proposal does not document creation of the project or relocation of its core team.

evidence.item: The White House described the Genesis Mission as a government-led effort to use AI for science, involving more than 15 federal agencies and distributed research resources.
evidence.shows: A substantial government AI initiative exists, but its stated organization and purpose do not establish that a core AGI-development team moved to a secure facility.

evidence.item: DefenseScoop reported that the Pentagon was moving classified AI workloads from Anthropic to other frontier model providers.
evidence.shows: Frontier models were being used on classified systems, but model deployment is not evidence that the core research team developing AGI relocated.

SA-061.thesis: Once established, the US government AGI project is integrally a defense project and cooperates extremely closely with the national-security state.
SA-061.bar: The established AGI development effort must have defense as an integral purpose and operate in extremely close cooperation with US national-security institutions. A conventional purchaser–vendor relationship or isolated security consultation alone is insufficient.
SA-061.actor: The US government AGI project and US defense, intelligence, and other national-security institutions.
